For the second time in five days, American forces hit Iranian military targets on Qeshm Island; the president, after landing in West Palm Beach, described Friday’s strike as minor and said the target was an air defense system knocked out in about fifteen minutes, maybe five; Iranian media reported two explosions in the Suza area; Central Command had released no account of its own at filing; and late Friday the command posted a reward offer of up to $20 million for information about Iran’s nuclear program.

Subjective
Clash Report — the president confirms a new strike on Qeshm Island

The president confirmed a new limited strike against an Iranian air defense system near Qeshm Island, speaking to reporters in West Palm Beach on Friday evening; Tasnim reported two missiles struck the island and IRNA cited witnesses who heard an aircraft before two projectiles struck the Suza area; no official Iranian damage assessment and no confirmed casualty figures had been released; and the precise relationship between the reported impacts and the American operation has not been independently established.

Subjective
Storysh — two missiles strike Qeshm Island, Tasnim reports

Washington and Cairo: the president said the American military carried out new limited strikes on Iran early on Saturday, targeting its air defense systems; Iranian media reported the sound of two explosions in the Suza area of Qeshm Island, in the Strait of Hormuz; and IRNA quoted local witnesses saying two projectiles struck the island after the sound of an aircraft was heard over it.

Subjective
KuCoin, carrying BlockBeats — a limited strike announced, a larger action considered

On November 6 the president told the media the United States had carried out a limited strike against Iran, destroying a small air defense system manufactured by Iran; Tasnim’s preliminary reports indicated two missiles struck Qeshm Island; two American officials revealed that some advisers have told the president the window for a major military operation is closing, urging action before the new Congress takes office in January; and the president has not yet decided whether to restart the larger strikes, per a White House official.

Subjective
Augerton — the president weighing renewed military action

Published November 6: the president said Thursday he would soon decide whether to launch new strikes on Iran, warning he might destroy what is left of the country; after meeting his national security advisers he weighed extending the campaign to ensure Iran could not revive its nuclear program; Axios reported the options included renewed attacks, continued economic pressure, or a deal requiring significant Iranian concessions; and he said Iran could need 25 years to recover from the damage already done.

Subjective
Democracy Docket — the Mississippi ballot fight, live

The live file from Jackson, carrying the Associated Press figures through Friday: Mr. Colom’s lead at 2,010 votes at 12:30 p.m., 2,493 at 4:37 p.m. on totals of 467,829 to 465,336, and 2,574 at 8:50 p.m. on totals of 467,930 to 465,356; the secretary of state’s office confirmed in August it had eliminated a rule allowing correction of mail ballots while the old rule remains on the state’s website; voters declared inactive after the state’s use of a credit reporting company to check its rolls describe casting affidavit ballots; and the counties certify by November 13.

Subjective
Associated Press, via KCAU — why it is still too early to call Mississippi

Nearly 2,500 votes separate Mr. Colom and Senator Hyde-Smith and votes are still being counted; the wire’s estimate of votes remaining stood at about 44,000 on Friday morning and was revised to about 30,000 by 4:45 p.m.; about 7 percent of ballots have yet to be counted in Hinds County, where Mr. Colom leads by roughly 47,000 votes; and about 2,200 votes are estimated outstanding in Rankin County.

Subjective
Queen City Newsfeed — Hyde-Smith says she is not backing down, at 2,498

Senator Hyde-Smith’s Friday message that she is not backing down, as the newest state numbers put Mr. Colom ahead by 2,498 votes, 467,846 to 465,348, on Friday afternoon; counties have reviewed 11,202 affidavit ballots statewide, of which 8,717 were accepted and 2,485 rejected; mail ballots count if they arrive by Tuesday, November 10; and county officials have until November 13 to certify.

Subjective
AmeriLedger — the Mississippi race still a toss-up, the Democrat holding a slim lead

With about 96 percent of the vote in, Mr. Colom’s lead grew from a few dozen votes on Wednesday morning to over 2,500 by Friday afternoon; the secretary of state said Friday there are approximately 3,300 outstanding mail ballots; several thousand ballots still need to be counted and both campaigns express confidence; and Mississippi does not allow recounts, so the winner is decided on a plurality of votes.

Subjective
WENG Radio — Mississippi undecided, no recount law on the books

The race remains undecided on Friday night with Mr. Colom holding a lead of roughly 2,500 votes; election officials are still working through mail-in and provisional ballots and the state Republican Party estimates about 20,000 ballots remain outstanding; provisional voters have until November 10 to resolve verification issues; Mississippi is the only state in the country without any provision for a recount; and the deadline to certify is November 13.

Subjective
Al Jazeera — what is delaying the Senate results in Mississippi and Alaska

An explainer of the two undecided Senate races: in Mississippi, provisional and mail-in ballots still to be processed within the state’s ten days, about 3,600 mail ballots counted outstanding on Wednesday with an unknown number of affidavit ballots, certification due November 13, and no formal recount provision without a court order; in Alaska, the distances and the ranked-choice system, the tally unchanged at 637 votes, tabulation results due November 18, the two candidates named Dan Sullivan, and the Justice Department’s dismissed suit over the second Sullivan, with an appeal pledged.

Subjective
Reason — Ms. Peltola appears likely to defeat both Dan Sullivans

With about three-fourths of Alaska’s votes tallied, Senator Sullivan trails Ms. Peltola by just over 600 votes; a New York Times analysis of the scanned ballots finds nearly 30 percent of the second Sullivan’s voters ranked Ms. Peltola second, and that even if all of that candidate’s voters who ranked no one else had intended the incumbent, he would gain only about one percentage point; the president’s post demanding the second Sullivan’s votes be given to the incumbent is quoted; the Justice Department’s dismissed suit is recorded; and the state must count all ballots by November 18.

Subjective
New York Post — Republicans count a few more House wins

The Associated Press had called 254 House races for the Democrats and 162 for the Republicans as of Friday afternoon, up from 155 Republican calls on Thursday, with 19 seats still open; Friday’s Republican calls were Representative Hurd in Colorado, Mr. Lamb in Arizona, and Mr. Constantino in New York’s 21st; the incumbents in danger include Representatives Boebert, Finstad, DesJarlais, and Foxx; and the Senate stands at 54 to 44 called, with Mr. Colom ahead by about 2,500 in Mississippi and Ms. Peltola by about 600 in Alaska.

Subjective
USA Today — the live file, November 6

The day’s running file: the Justice Department drops its attempt to set aside 20,000 California ballots, at 8:10 p.m.; Ms. Lacore flips South Carolina’s 1st District, at 8:35 p.m.; Houston’s mayor directs police to reduce cooperation with federal immigration authorities, at 9:57 p.m.; Mr. Mann defeats Attorney General Kobach in Kansas, at 10:40 p.m.; Mr. Colom’s lead passes 2,500, at 6:43 p.m.; incoming Senate Democrats question Mr. Schumer’s leadership and he answers, at 7:23 p.m.; three Justice Department officials resign across Thursday and Friday, at 5:30 p.m.; and Mr. Miller is named chief of staff, at 2:11 p.m.

Subjective
Associated Press, via Now Georgia — the Justice Department drops its California ballot bid

Los Angeles: the department on Friday moved to dismiss its own lawsuit seeking to stop California from counting roughly 20,000 ballots it alleged went to noncitizens; the dismissal comes days after the midterm losses and about a week before a special master was to evaluate the accuracy of the government’s list; California had processed roughly 9 million ballots by early Friday with nearly 5 million left; the motion states the challenged ballots will have been commingled with lawful ones; and the department’s Alaska suit, swiftly dismissed, is under an appeal not yet fully briefed.

Subjective
Reuters, via Duke FM — the administration ends the California balloting lawsuit

November 6: the administration withdrew its lawsuit attempting to block California from counting mail-in ballots from more than 20,000 registered voters federal officials alleged were likely non-citizens; the notice of voluntary dismissal was filed after an election in which Democrats won California’s statewide contests and most of its congressional races; the Supreme Court on Monday rejected a bid to block the counting temporarily; and the department’s filing states the relief sought is no longer available now that the votes have been tallied.

Subjective
Market Briefer — the global close, November 6

The Nasdaq Composite rose 1.09 percent to 24,579.42 and the S&P 500 0.31 percent to 7,376.86 as chips rebounded, while the Dow fell 0.46 percent to 51,285.73; October payrolls of 165,000 lifted the priced probability of a December rate increase to about 78 percent and the ten-year yield to 4.86 percent; the week closed down 2.7 percent for the S&P 500, 3.4 percent for the Nasdaq, and 0.9 percent for the Dow; and the Nikkei 225 fell 5.96 percent to 57,434.77, more than 20 percent below its late-June record.

Subjective
World Money Roadmap — the weekly market file

Friday brought a partial bounce in chips and a hot jobs report: the Nasdaq Composite closed the week at 24,579.42, down 3.37 percent, and the S&P 500 at 7,376.86, down 2.68 percent, its worst week since June; payrolls rose 165,000 against a 59,000 consensus, unemployment slipped to 4.1 percent, and the prior two months were revised up by a combined 84,000; and the closes are stated per CNBC, with weekly changes calculated from the October 30 closes.

Subjective
Capp Notes, Substack — the closing look, Friday, November 6

Stocks finished mixed as the artificial-intelligence and chip names bounced, recovering part of Thursday’s selloff; the Nasdaq-100 rose 1.35 percent, the Nasdaq Composite 1.09 percent to 24,579.42, the S&P 500 0.31 percent to 7,376.86, and the Dow fell 0.46 percent to 51,285.73; the hot October jobs report lifted rate-increase odds and the dollar while leaving the S&P 500 down about 2.7 percent on the week; and the volatility index fell sharply from Thursday’s spike.

Subjective
Market Briefer — Corporate America, November 6

Chips rebounded Friday after Thursday’s rout as payrolls tripled the forecasts at 165,000; Moderna and Vistra beat and raised their outlooks and DraftKings fell 21 percent on the cost of its prediction-markets venture; the Associated Press close is recorded at 24,579.42 for the Nasdaq, 7,376.86 for the S&P 500, and 51,285.73 for the Dow; and the one to watch for Saturday, November 7, is Berkshire Hathaway’s third-quarter earnings release and Form 10-Q, at about 7:00 a.m. Central.

Subjective
Associated Press — Senate, every state

The Senate file in its latest state: 35 races listed, Alaska and Mississippi both too early to call, and the remaining races called state by state; the chamber stands at 54 seats for the Democrats and 44 for the Republicans in the called races.

Subjective
The Coloradoan — when the 4th District result will be seen

Updated at about 2 p.m. on November 6: Representative Boebert trails Ms. Laubacher by 3,278 votes, 48.78 percent to 47.92, with the Libertarian at 3.31 percent; at least 5,000 ballots remain in the four most populous counties by the account’s estimate; 474 district ballots await signature cure; and an automatic recount would be triggered at about 926 votes.

Subjective
MySourceLine — the Mississippi count watch

A running tally of the race by outlet and hour: Mr. Colom’s lead at 1,813 in the ABC News results early Friday, 2,010 in the Associated Press count at midday Friday, and nearly 2,500 in the wire’s Friday-afternoon story, with the wire estimating about 30,000 votes still to count at 4:45 p.m.; the counts are stated to be news counts, not official, and no outlet has called the race.
items.summary: The midnight file for Saturday, November 7, 2026: the United States struck an air-defense installation on Qeshm Island on Friday evening and the president called it minor while the larger Iran decision stayed unannounced, Mississippi's Democratic lead widened to 2,574 votes with Alaska unchanged at 637, the Justice Department dropped its California ballot lawsuit, the House called more races on Friday, and the worst week for stocks since June closed split. Collected at 0000.

items.title: The Chips Bounce Back, the Count Does Not Move, and No Decision Comes
items.content_html:
The Evening File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

The Chips Bounce Back, the Count Does Not Move, and No Decision Comes

The day’s developments whole at 1800: the morning’s payrolls beat stands as the day’s largest settled fact, New York closes mixed with technology up and the Dow down, the semiconductor index recovers about a third of Thursday’s fall, a Federal Reserve president says more tightening is likely, Europe closes lower across the board, no race is called for a third day, and the two decisions the week is waiting on—Iran in Washington, the count in Mississippi and Alaska—are both still waiting at evening.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1800 ET, Friday, November 6, 2026. This edition completes the day continued in Edition No. 10, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400, and Edition No. 11, the Midday Watch, collected at 1200. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the evening figures differ from the noon figures, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Evening in Brief

Friday corrected Thursday in the labor report and did not correct it in the count. The October payrolls figure printed at midday stands at the close: 165,000 jobs added, against a consensus near 60,000, unemployment at 4.1 percent, and the two prior months revised up by a combined 84,000. Around that fact the afternoon produced its considered responses. The chip shares that fell twelve percent on Thursday recovered about four percent. The Dow closed lower for the day and the Nasdaq higher, a split that held from the opening bell to the close. San Francisco’s Federal Reserve president, speaking after the payrolls, said the central bank will probably have to tighten further. Europe, which had no payrolls report of its own, closed down about one percent. In the count, Mississippi’s Democratic lead stands near 2,000 votes in the afternoon tallies, Alaska’s stands unchanged at 637 with its next update set for Tuesday, and Colorado’s 4th District stands wider, at 3,278 votes in the state’s afternoon figures. No race was called. On Iran, no decision was announced. On Ukraine, the Kremlin’s answer stands at no details, and Kyiv’s president asked for guarantees clear on paper. The desk files those in that order.

The Markets at the Close: A Bounce, Not a Recovery

New York closed in the split it opened in. The week’s closing account, in the market recap of November 2 to 6 filed below, puts Friday’s closes at 7,376.86 for the S&P 500, up 0.3 percent; 24,579.42 for the Nasdaq Composite, up 1.1 percent; and 51,285.73 for the Dow Jones Industrial Average, down 0.5 percent. The post-market scorecard carries the same Dow close, 51,285.73, down 0.46 percent, with the Nasdaq 100 up 1.36 percent and the volatility index down 9 percent to 25.64. A second closing account, carrying Investing.com’s figures, runs the day a shade stronger—the Dow down 0.26 percent, the S&P 500 up 0.65 percent, the Nasdaq up 1.46 percent, and the volatility index down 14.25 percent to 24.14. The two accounts differ in the last digits and agree on the shape: technology and the broad index up, the Dow down, fear down from Thursday’s close of 28.09 and still above every level of the week before the election.

The chips recovered part of Thursday, and the part is stated plainly. The semiconductor index advanced 4.2 percent on Friday after falling more than 12 percent on Thursday, per the rebound account filed below, which puts the Nasdaq Composite up 1.71 percent at its hour. Advanced Micro Devices led the recovery: up 11.0 percent at the close in the market data filed below, after a fall of 17.3 percent on Thursday, and up about 8 percent in the morning account in the chip file, which has Intel up 5 percent and Micron up 8 percent at its hour. Nvidia closed up 2.8 percent in the same market data, after rising about 6 percent in early trading and falling 9.3 percent on Thursday. No account on the shelf describes Friday as a recovery of the week. The week’s totals in the recap are the standing measure: the S&P 500 down 2.7 percent, the Nasdaq Composite down 3.4 percent, and the Dow down 0.9 percent—stocks’ worst week since June, in that account’s words, made of a Wednesday rally, a Thursday rout that erased it, and a Friday bounce that recovered a fraction of the rout.

Europe closed lower, and its close is the day’s plainest contrast with New York. The pan-European STOXX 600 closed down 1 percent at 648.33, with insurance the leading faller, down 2.6 percent, and travel the only rising sector, up 0.9 percent, per Reuters’ closing file. The closing wrap puts the national closes in a row: Germany’s DAX down 1.92 percent at 25,820.37, France’s CAC 40 down 0.81 percent at 8,139.01, Britain’s FTSE 100 down 1.01 percent at 10,673.93, Spain’s IBEX down 0.60 percent, and Italy’s FTSE MIB down 0.90 percent. Teleperformance closed down 15.3 percent in the Reuters file, after cutting its revenue outlook—the same name that led the midday fall at 18 percent. Europe fell on the day the American technology shares rose. The midday edition printed the shelter argument, that Europe’s smaller share of the AI trade cushions it; at the close the cushion held in degree, as it held at noon, and the direction was down in every market on the continent’s list.

The Rate File at Evening: More Tightening Is Likely, in One President’s Expectation

The afternoon’s new voice on rates is San Francisco’s, and she spoke after the payrolls. Mary Daly, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, said on Friday that the central bank will probably have to tighten policy further. “My expectation is we’re going to have to tighten policy further,” she said in a television interview carried in the account of her remarks filed below, adding that exactly when and how much is still to be decided. She called the payrolls report good news for American workers, said she favors a gradual approach, and said she is prepared to act if the economy calls for it. Reuters’ account of the same interview adds her description of the week’s technology repricing as painful but orderly. Ms. Daly does not vote on the rate-setting committee this year; she votes next year. Her sentence is filed as her expectation, stated on the day the labor report beat every forecast on the shelf.

New York’s president, speaking in Frankfurt before the report, took the other half of the same position. John Williams said inflation is absolutely too high and has been too high for too long, and that it is essential to bring it back to the 2 percent target in a timely manner, per Reuters’ Frankfurt file. He did not discuss the next move, and said the committee’s last statement had correctly concluded that it was appropriate to collect more information. The two statements together are the central bank’s Friday whole: the goal stated without qualification in Frankfurt, the likely means stated as an expectation in San Francisco, and the timing left open by both. The market’s own reading stands where the midday edition left it, firmer after the payrolls: the probability of a quarter-point increase at the December 8–9 meeting above three in four in the CME FedWatch readings carried at noon, the range standing at 3.75 to 4.00 percent, and October consumer prices, due Tuesday, November 10, as the next bearing. Gold closed the week on the other side of that reading, down on the day in every account—at $4,064.50, down $38, in the closing newsletter, and at $4,061.30, down 1.17 percent against a prior close of $4,109.45, in the macro report timed 1800 UTC.

Oil and the Strait at Evening

Oil ended the week where the midday seesaw left it: under $100 in the London states, over it in the Asian morning, and down by a double-digit figure on the week in every file. The London Reuters file carried at midday—January Brent down 0.8 percent at $97.55 and West Texas Intermediate down 0.8 percent at $89.79 by 0826 GMT, with Brent on track for a fall of 16 percent on the week—stands joined at evening by the weekly account filed below, which carries the same London figures and the same 16 percent measure, the steepest weekly percentage fall since the start of the pandemic in that file. The Asian files put the week at about 12 percent. No single Friday settlement figure appears in more than one file the desk took in by 1800, and the desk does not print one as settled. Thursday’s settlement stands beneath the week as its last agreed fixed point: Brent $98.29, West Texas Intermediate $90.52. The cargo in the price is unchanged from noon: de-escalation hopes after the election pulling down, tanker incidents holding a floor, and flows through the strait under 60 percent of capacity.

The strait file grew by a claim on Friday, and the claim stands unconfirmed at evening. The Revolutionary Guards said two more oil tankers struck naval mines and caught fire while crossing the strait by an unauthorized route, in the statement the midday edition filed. The account of the claim filed below adds the particulars the statement carried—one vessel east of the strait and a second inside it, both said to have switched off their transponders, the statement posted at 0758 GMT and carried by Mehr News Agency—and the standing answer beside it: no confirmation of any incident from maritime officials, and no confirmation from the American military, the British agency, or any flag authority of the mine strikes described in the Guards’ recent announcements. The British agency’s count of at least five vessels reporting incidents since Sunday stands as the last confirmed tally. The claims are filed as claims, as this paper has filed them all week. What is confirmed at evening is narrower: 129 incidents in the strait and the wider region documented by the International Maritime Organization as of November 6, in the same account’s figures, and a strait Tehran says remains closed until its seven conditions are met.

The Count at Evening: Nothing Called, Mississippi Near Two Thousand

No Senate race was called on Friday, for the third full day. The Associated Press Senate file in its latest state still lists Alaska and Mississippi as too early to call, and the chamber stands at 54 seats for the Democrats and 44 for the Republicans. The House count moved at the edges without a call of consequence in the afternoon. The live House file, updated at 1:28 p.m. EST, runs 254 seats called for the Democrats and 164 for the Republicans, with eight more led by the Democrats and nine by the Republicans, 418 of 435 races called. The tally carrying NBC News’ calls runs it lower: 250 for the Democrats and 161 for the Republicans, with 24 uncalled, and an estimated final of 259 to 176 if the leads hold. The wire’s tracker at midday stood at 249 won and 12 led. Three desks, three hours, one chamber, and agreement on the outcome and on nothing smaller—the sentence this paper has printed every day of the count, because every day of the count has made it true again.

Mississippi’s margin stands near 2,000 votes in the afternoon tallies, and the afternoon’s news in the race is money and procedure. The Caller’s account, carrying the Associated Press figures of early Friday afternoon, puts the Democrat, Scott Colom, at 49.1 percent and the incumbent Republican, Cindy Hyde-Smith, at 48.8 percent, with more than 95 percent counted and a lead of about 2,000 votes. The state account filed below puts the lead at 1,936 after a Friday-morning return from Bolivar County added a net 123 votes, and at 2,010 in a subsequent state report. The midday edition’s newest tally stood at 2,087. The range at evening is therefore 1,936 to 2,087, the leader the same in every state of it. The procedure stands as filed: mailed absentee ballots postmarked by Election Day must arrive by November 10, affidavit ballots are being verified at the county level, and counties certify by November 13. The new entries are the parties’ preparations for the finish: both Senate campaign committees have created recount funds, per the Caller’s account, and the Republican committee has written to Mississippi’s county election officials demanding that affidavit ballots be separated and preserved. The race is being prepared for a dispute before it has produced a loser.

Alaska did not move, and the argument about Alaska did. The tally stands where it has stood since Wednesday: the Democrat, Mary Peltola, ahead of the incumbent Republican, Dan Sullivan, by 637 first-choice votes, with the next major update expected Tuesday, November 10, when more early and absentee ballots are added, and the ranked-choice tabulation set for November 18 if no candidate holds a majority. The afternoon’s new material is the Sullivan campaign’s arithmetic, carried in the Caller’s account: if the ranked-choice tabulation were run today on the votes in hand, the campaign states, Mr. Sullivan would defeat Ms. Peltola 105,037 to 104,709, a margin of 328, because the second candidate named Daniel Sullivan’s voters are expected to rank the incumbent second. The statement is the campaign’s. It is printed beside the standing facts that cut the other way in the same account: about 20,000 early votes and 27,000 absentee ballots in hand and not yet counted, late mail and questioned ballots still to come, and a New York Times analysis, carried in the state account, suggesting Ms. Peltola could retain her advantage after tabulation. Two projections of one unrun tabulation, filed as projections. The count itself will speak on November 18, or sooner if the ballots arriving Tuesday settle the first-choice majority.

Colorado’s 4th District widened in the afternoon, and the trailing campaign’s position hardened with it. The state account updated at about 2 p.m. puts the Democrat, Eileen Laubacher, ahead of the incumbent Republican, Lauren Boebert, by 3,278 votes—48.78 percent to 47.92—wider than the 3,069 in the wire’s midday totals and the 3,024 in the state’s Thursday-night figures. The automatic recount line stands at about 926 votes, and the margin is more than three times it. What remains, in the same account: at least 5,000 ballots still to be counted in the district’s four most populous counties by its estimate, 474 ballots awaiting signature cure, and the cure and military-ballot deadline of November 12, with counties finishing November 13. The district account filed below carries the Boebert campaign’s lawyer’s statement of late Thursday—the campaign is investigating what it calls unusual voting patterns and expects a recount one way or another—and notes that a recount at this margin is paid for by the candidate who asks for it. The race is uncalled. The path the remaining ballots would have to take is narrower at evening than it was at noon, and the campaign’s stated intention has not narrowed with it.

Washington at Evening: The Leadership Field Is Set

The noon deadline for the House Republican leadership races passed with the field as it stood on Wednesday. No new name entered in any file the desk took in during the afternoon. The contest for minority leader stands as filed: Majority Leader Steve Scalise and Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, both declared since Wednesday, with Speaker Mike Johnson not seeking the post. Majority Whip Tom Emmer seeks to remain whip, challenged by August Pfluger. The conference elects on Tuesday, November 10, by secret ballot, per the account of the contest filed below and the election’s record. The same account carries the business that waits for whoever wins: Republicans hold both chambers until January and must pass a measure funding the government past December, and the winner inherits the conference’s response to the incoming majority’s investigations. Mr. Scalise’s Thursday letter asking committee chairs to take inventory of the expected investigations, filed at midday, and Mr. Jordan’s letter pitching himself as battle-tested for them, are the two campaigns’ documents of record at evening. The House itself returns Monday. In the Senate, the Republican leadership election is also set for November 10, with Majority Leader John Thune expected to run again, per the accounts filed earlier this week. Nothing in Washington was decided on Friday except the shape of Tuesday.

The Two Capitals’ Files: No Decision on Iran, No Details on Ukraine

On Iran, the decision the president promised on Thursday had not been announced at 1800 on Friday, and the preparations reported around it are preparations. The fullest account of the Thursday meeting filed below records the president’s words in the Oval Office after his first post-midterm national security meeting: a decision is coming, the choice is whether to go further with strikes until Iran’s nuclear program can, in his word, be certified dead, or to stop short of destroying what is left of the country. “I would rather not destroy the rest of the country if possible, but maybe I’ll have to. You’ll know soon enough.” The same account and the day’s operations file record the standing military fact beside the words: Central Command is finalizing preparations to potentially resume major combat operations and has received no new directive. Readiness is not an order. The carrier arithmetic is also in the files: the Theodore Roosevelt strike group is stopping in Singapore from Friday and will not reach the region before mid-November. On the diplomatic track, the Qatari draft and Iran’s formal nuclear proposal, sent through Qatar on Thursday and under review in Washington, stand as the overnight and midday editions printed them, with Tehran’s seven conditions unmet and unwithdrawn. Rapidan Energy Group’s Bob McNally puts the chance of fighting resuming at 80 percent, in the operations file’s figure. That is an analyst’s probability, filed as one. At evening the war’s state is the state of Thursday night, one day older: a decision promised, not made; a proposal delivered, not answered; a strait claimed closed, with traffic under 60 percent of capacity.

On Ukraine, Friday added Kyiv’s asking price to Thursday’s distance between Washington and Moscow. The president’s Thursday description stands: an agreement that is going to be big, that could involve more than Ukraine and all of Europe, with no terms and no timeline given. The Kremlin spokesman’s Friday answer stands beside it, in the account of his briefing: there are no details; the envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, has not yet returned or reported to President Putin; and no European proposals on security guarantees have reached Moscow. The new statement is Ukraine’s. President Zelenskyy, in an interview aired late Thursday after two days of allied talks in Brussels on postwar security and reconstruction, said his government wants guarantees clear on paper: “If Russia starts attacking again, what will happen? Who will do what, with what means, and when?” per the Associated Press account filed below. He said he believes Ukraine’s chances of additional American assistance may now grow after the midterm results. The American envoys’ framework is also in the record: five goals, including permanent security consultations and no country holding a veto over another’s alliances, in the account of the envoys’ post filed below, with the Kremlin’s standing position that guarantees can only be mutual. Delegations from Washington, Moscow, and Kyiv meet in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11, the first trilateral talks since February, with Vladimir Medinsky leading Russia’s team. Three positions are now on paper where one description stood on Thursday: Washington’s big agreement without details, Moscow’s no details without an agreement, and Kyiv’s demand that whatever is agreed be written down in advance. Abu Dhabi is four days away.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. First, New York’s close: the S&P 500 up 0.3 percent at 7,376.86 in the week’s recap, up 0.65 percent in the second closing account, and up 0.62 percent at 7,399.32 in the late-afternoon prints—one rising day read at three hours, with the Dow’s close agreed at 51,285.73 in two accounts and its fall put at 0.26 percent in a third. Second, Mississippi: 1,936 in the state account’s morning return, 2,010 in its later report, about 2,000 in the wire’s afternoon figures, and 2,087 in the midday tally—four readings of one lead, the leader unchanged in each. Third, Brent’s week: down about 12 percent in the Asian files and down 16 percent in the London file, with no Friday settlement agreed across the shelf by 1800. Fourth, gold’s close: $4,064.50 in one closing account and $4,061.30 in another, down on the day in both. Against the triangle, the load-bearing facts of the evening are single-valued: payrolls rose 165,000 and unemployment fell to 4.1 percent; the semiconductor index recovered 4.2 percent of Thursday’s 12 percent fall; Europe’s STOXX 600 closed down 1 percent at 648.33; the week closed down 2.7 percent for the S&P 500, 3.4 percent for the Nasdaq, and 0.9 percent for the Dow; no race was called; Colorado’s 4th stands at 3,278 in the state’s afternoon figures; the House Republican leadership field closed at noon with two names; San Francisco’s president expects more tightening; no Iran decision was announced; and Tuesday, November 10, now carries the payrolls’ successor bearing in consumer prices, Mississippi’s ballot deadline, Alaska’s next update, both parties’ leadership elections in the House, and the opening of the Abu Dhabi talks. The log proceeds to midnight.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. Thirty-one items.

Subjective
Pioneer Advice — the week’s market recap, November 2–6

Stocks had their worst week since June: the S&P 500 fell 2.7 percent to 7,376.86, the Nasdaq Composite 3.4 percent to 24,579.42, and the Dow 0.9 percent to 51,285.73; Friday is recorded as hot jobs and a partial bounce, with payrolls at 165,000 against about 65,000 expected, yields up, a December hike as the market’s base case, chips rebounding, and the Dow slipping.

Subjective
PrimeXBT, carrying Investing.com — the Dow slips as the Nasdaq and the S&P gain

The Dow closed Friday down 0.26 percent while the S&P 500 climbed 0.65 percent and the Nasdaq Composite 1.46 percent; technology, industrials, and consumer goods led the gains; Nvidia rose 3.61 percent to 188.15 within the Dow; Airbnb rose 12.03 percent and AMD 11.48 percent to 450.82 among S&P names; and the volatility index fell 14.25 percent to 24.14.

Subjective
Shunya.Trade — the session scorecard, November 6

The post-market review: the Nasdaq 100 at 27,116.50, up 1.36 percent; the Dow at 51,285.73, down 0.46 percent; the volatility index at 25.64, down 9.01 percent; gold futures at 4,074.60, down 0.95 percent; and crude oil at 90.48, down 0.04 percent.

Subjective
FundSpec — the market edition, November 6

The last index prints at 15:35 ET: the Dow at 51,382.54, down 0.27 percent; the Nasdaq Composite at 24,667.08, up 1.45 percent; and the S&P 500 at 7,399.32, up 0.62 percent; fifty companies on the day’s earnings calendar, all reported, twenty-five above estimate.

Subjective
SKN — the Nasdaq rebounds as semiconductors recover

The Nasdaq Composite gained 1.71 percent to 24,730.30 at its hour, supported by semiconductor shares after Thursday’s steep decline; the broader semiconductor index advanced 4.2 percent after falling more than 12 percent; Nvidia gained 3.8 percent, and AMD, Intel, and Micron rose between 6 and 10 percent.

Subjective
Summa Money — AMD jumps, Intel and Nvidia climb, as chips rebound

AMD at $437.11, up 8 percent in morning trading after Thursday’s 17 percent drop, and still down 33 percent over the past month; Intel at $55.09, up 5 percent after a 10 percent slide; Nvidia at $189.80, up 5 percent after a 9 percent decline; Micron up 8 percent; and the semiconductor index’s 12 percent fall on November 5 recorded as its worst sell-off since 2020.

Subjective
The Private Banker — Daly says more tightening is likely after the payrolls beat

San Francisco President Mary Daly, hours after the 165,000 payrolls report: her expectation is that the central bank will have to tighten policy further, with when and how much still to be decided; the report is good news for American workers; she favors a gradual approach and is prepared to act; and the December hike odds are put at roughly 77 percent after the data.

Subjective
Reuters, via KSEV — Daly says a rate hike is likely, despite the tech-stock dive

November 6: President Daly said she feels the central bank will likely need to raise rates further to bring too-high inflation down, while acknowledging what she called the painful but orderly repricing of technology stocks as investors reassess the risks to AI-driven demand growth.

Subjective
Reuters, via Kitco — Williams: inflation too high, essential to get back to 2 percent

Frankfurt, November 6: New York President John Williams said economic growth has remained resilient and the labor market remarkably stable, but inflation is absolutely too high and has been too high for too long; he did not discuss the next move and said the last statement correctly concluded it was appropriate to collect more information.

Subjective
Reuters, via Duke FM — Williams in Frankfurt

The same Frankfurt remarks in a second file: inflation too high and to be brought back to 2 percent in a timely manner and on a sustained basis; the economy resilient and the labor market remarkably stable despite successive shocks; and financial markets seeing a more than 50 percent chance of a December hike, with a move by March fully priced.

Subjective
Reuters, via Devdiscourse — risk-off mood sweeps European stocks

European shares fell 1 percent on Friday and the STOXX 600 closed at 648.33, with the German benchmark down 1.9 percent; insurance fell 2.6 percent, with Hannover Re down 4.3 percent, Munich Re down 4.4 percent, and Swiss Re down 4.6 percent; Teleperformance slumped 15.3 percent; Orsted rose 1.2 percent and Nordex 5 percent; and travel stocks were the only sector to rise, adding 0.9 percent.

Subjective
InvestingLive — European stocks fall into the weekend as Wall Street rebounds

The European closes: the DAX at 25,820.37, down 1.92 percent on the day and unchanged for the week; the CAC 40 at 8,139.01, down 0.81 percent and up 2.13 percent for the week; the FTSE 100 at 10,673.93, down 1.01 percent; the IBEX at 19,369.49, down 0.60 percent and up 3.84 percent for the week; and the FTSE MIB at 50,052.95, down 0.90 percent.

Subjective
Reuters, via Duke FM — European shares fall as the rout gathers pace

November 6: the STOXX 600 dropped 1 percent to 648.83 by 0919 GMT, wiping out its gains for the week; media, health care, and personal and household goods fell over 2 percent each; Teleperformance tanked 18 percent at its hour; Orsted rose 2.7 percent, Nordex 1.7 percent, and EDP 1.6 percent; and the index’s smaller AI exposure is stated as its relative shelter.

Subjective
GoldDealer — the daily gold newsletter, November 6

Commentary for Friday, November 6, 2026: gold closed down $38.00 at $4,064.50, and silver closed down $0.43 at $51.80.

Subjective
RM Intelligence — the gold macro report, November 6

Compiled November 6 at 1800 UTC: spot gold at 4,061.30, down 48.15, or 1.17 percent, against the prior session close of 4,109.45; the regime read is defensive; and the managed-money positioning figures are carried from the report of October 27 and stated to be stale.

Subjective
Energy News Africa, carrying Reuters — oil heads for its biggest weekly drop since 2020

Brent for January fell 74 cents, or 0.8 percent, to $97.55 by 0826 GMT and West Texas Intermediate slipped 73 cents to $89.79; Brent is on course for a 16 percent weekly decline, its steepest percentage fall since the start of the pandemic and its biggest in absolute terms in data back to 1988; and prices tumbled 8 percent on Wednesday alone after the midterm results.

Subjective
House of Saud — the Guards claim two more tankers hit mines in Hormuz

The Revolutionary Guards’ Friday claim that two more tankers struck mines and caught fire, one east of the strait and one inside it, both said to have switched off their transponders; Brent near $99 on Friday morning after Thursday’s settlement at $98.29; the weekly loss put at 12 to 16 percent; the maritime organization’s count of 129 incidents and 25 seafarer fatalities; and the statement that no American, British, or flag authority has confirmed the mine strikes.

Subjective
Associated Press — Senate, every state

The Senate file in its latest state: 35 races listed, Alaska and Mississippi both too early to call, and the remaining races called state by state.

Subjective
Poliwave — the House live results file

Updated November 6 at 1:28 p.m. EST: 254 House seats called for the Democrats and 164 for the Republicans, with eight more led by the Democrats and nine by the Republicans, 418 of 435 races called.

Subjective
BeeBulletin, carrying NBC News — the midterm results so far

Updated November 6: NBC News has called 250 House seats for the Democrats and 161 for the Republicans, with 24 uncalled, and estimates a final 259 to 176 if the leads hold; the Senate stands called at 54 to 44; and tallies are stated to differ between outlets and to change as races are called.

Subjective
Daily Caller — both parties raise recount funds as the counting persists

Days after the polls closed, both Senate campaign committees have created recount funds; the Associated Press figures of early Friday afternoon put Colom ahead by about 2,000 votes at 49.1 percent to 48.8 percent in Mississippi, with more than 95 percent counted, and Peltola ahead at 48.17 percent to 47.8 percent in Alaska with 74 percent counted; the Republican committee’s letter demanding affidavit ballots be separated and preserved; and the Sullivan campaign’s statement that a ranked-choice tabulation run today would put Sullivan ahead 105,037 to 104,709.

Subjective
The Rico TV — a new ballot return shifts the Mississippi Senate race

Colom’s lead pushed to 1,936 votes on Friday morning after returns from Bolivar County gave him a net gain of 123, and to 2,010 in a subsequent state report; the contest remained uncalled with absentee and affidavit ballots still being processed; mailed ballots postmarked by Election Day must arrive by November 10 and counties certify by November 13; and Alaska’s tally is recorded unchanged, with its next major update expected Tuesday.

Subjective
The Coloradoan — when the 4th District result will be seen

Updated at about 2 p.m. on November 6: Boebert trails Laubacher by 3,278 votes, 48.78 percent to 47.92, with the Libertarian at 3.31 percent; at least 5,000 ballots remain in the four most populous counties by the account’s estimate; 474 district ballots await signature cure; and an automatic recount would be triggered at about 926 votes.

Subjective
American Muckrakers — the 4th District update: the lead grows to 3,069

The wire’s Friday-midday totals: Laubacher 184,624, Boebert 181,555, the Libertarian 12,506, a lead of 3,069 on 378,685 counted; the state’s Thursday-night figures at 3,024; the Boebert campaign lawyer’s statement that the campaign is investigating unusual voting patterns; the cure and military deadline of November 12; and a projection of a final margin near 3,900, in a stated range of 2,800 to 4,600.

Subjective
Christianity Now — Johnson steps aside, Jordan and Scalise seek the post

Washington, November 5: House Republicans choose a new leader on November 10 after Speaker Johnson decided against seeking the minority leader post; candidates had until noon on November 6 to declare; Jordan’s and Scalise’s letters to colleagues are recorded; Jeffries has formally launched his bid for speaker; and the lame-duck funding measure past December is named as the business ahead.

Subjective
Wikipedia — the 2026 House Republican Conference leadership election

The election’s record: the conference votes November 10, 2026, before the 120th Congress; representatives had until November 6 to declare; Scalise and Jordan are the declared candidates for minority leader, with their districts and present posts; Speaker Johnson has ruled out a run; and one incumbent committee chair’s re-election had yet to be called as of November 6.

Subjective
Signal Post News — the Iran war decision: “Maybe I’ll have to”

Washington, November 6: the president, after his first post-midterm national security meeting, said he will soon decide whether to resume all-out war, laid out the choice as going further until the nuclear program can be certified dead or stopping short of destroying the rest of the country, and said no new strikes have been ordered and no decision announced; Central Command is finalizing preparations without a new directive; and the Theodore Roosevelt group’s Singapore stop and mid-November arrival are recorded.

Subjective
GlobalSecurity.org — the Iran war, day 252 update, November 6

The operations file with a 0500 ET cutoff: the president weighing resumed operations and Central Command finalizing preparations without a directive; officials noting November 9 is a new moon; Iran’s formal nuclear proposal sent through Qatar, with its seven demands including compensation, an end to sanctions and the blockade, release of frozen assets, and a permanent end to the war; Rapidan’s Bob McNally putting the chance of fighting resuming at 80 percent; and 18 Americans stated killed in total.

Subjective
Silent Dossier — why the Kremlin says it has no details on the deal

November 6: spokesman Peskov’s answer in three words, there are no details; Dmitriev has not yet returned from the United States or reported to President Putin; no European ideas on security guarantees have reached Russia; the White House event marking the Oleshky ceasefire is described; and delegations from Washington, Moscow, and Kyiv are due in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11.

Subjective
Associated Press, via Military.com — Zelenskyy presses allies for clear postwar guarantees

Kyiv: President Zelenskyy seeks specific guarantees, clear on paper, on what happens if Russia attacks again—who will do what, with what means, and when; the comments followed two days of Brussels talks on postwar security, reconstruction, and 2027 funding; lead negotiator Umerov’s post on the threats discussed is quoted; and Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s chances of additional American assistance may now grow.

Subjective
bne IntelliNews, via EuropeSays — the United States offers European security talks but no veto

No country would hold a veto over another’s alliances in a new framework, envoy Kushner said on November 5, listing five goals including permanent consultations, crisis communications, military transparency, and reciprocal de-escalation measures; Peskov’s November 3 statement that guarantees can only be mutual is carried; the Abu Dhabi meeting is put at working level on November 10–11 with Medinsky leading Russia’s team; and European leaders meet in Berlin on November 19.
items.summary: The evening file for November 6, 2026: New York closes mixed with the Nasdaq up and the Dow down, the chips recover part of Thursday's fall, San Francisco's president says more tightening is likely, Europe closes lower, Mississippi stands near 2,000 votes, Colorado's 4th widens to 3,278, and no Iran decision is announced. Collected at 1800.

items.title: Payrolls Triple the Forecast, the Chips Bounce, and Mississippi Widens
items.content_html:
The Midday File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

Payrolls Triple the Forecast, the Chips Bounce, and Mississippi Widens

At noon the morning has corrected the week in three places. The October payrolls report, the test the Overnight Watch left at 0830, came in at 165,000 jobs against a consensus of 59,000, with unemployment down to 4.1 percent and the two prior months revised up by 84,000. New York opened split and an hour in the chips were bouncing and the Dow was not. And the count corrected itself in the open: Mississippi’s margin is wider in the newest tally, Colorado’s 4th stands at 3,069 in the wire’s latest totals, and no race was called in the morning.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1200 ET, Friday, November 6, 2026. This edition continues Edition No. 10, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400. Where the noon figures differ from the overnight figures, the difference is stated here, in the open; the overnight edition stands unrevised, as a log stands.

The Noon in Brief

The morning’s largest settled fact is a labor report, not a market move. Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported at 0830, against forecasts of 59,000 in the Dow Jones consensus and 65,000 in the Reuters poll. The unemployment rate fell to 4.1 percent from 4.2. September’s gain, first printed at 29,000 in every edition of this paper since it was released, is revised to 60,000, and August’s to 186,000. The correction is filed where corrections belong, at the top of the next edition. Around that fact the morning arranged itself: the Nasdaq bounced on chip buying and the Dow did not follow; Europe fell at its midday by more than the overnight futures had promised; Brent seesawed across $100 and back under it; gold fell for a second session; the odds of a December rate increase rose from about two in three to better than three in four; and in Washington and Moscow the official statements of the morning were, in order, a deadline reached in the House Republican leadership race and a spokesman saying there are no details.

The Payrolls: 165,000, and the Record Corrected Upward

The report beat the highest forecast on the shelf, not only the consensus. CNN’s account of the release and USA Today’s account carry the same headline figures: 165,000 jobs added in October, unemployment at 4.1 percent, and combined upward revisions of 84,000 to August and September—August up 53,000 to 186,000, September up 31,000 to 60,000. The release file adds the detail under the headline: private payrolls up 159,000 against 64,000 expected, and the unrounded unemployment rate at 4.141 percent against 4.1753 percent the month before. The three-month average gain now stands at 137,000. The September figure this paper carried at 29,000 for five weeks was the bureau’s first estimate; the bureau’s second estimate is 60,000, and the log records the change rather than quietly replacing it.

The hiring was led by the services that employ the most people. Professional and business services added 70,000 jobs, against a prior-year average of 15,000 a month in the accounts; health care added 42,000, transportation and warehousing 25,000, and manufacturing 19,000, per the market account carrying the report’s breakdown. Average hourly earnings rose 14 cents, or 0.4 percent, to $38.00, and 3.1 percent over the year—the strongest monthly wage gain since January in one account, and above the 0.3 percent and 2.9 percent the forecasts had carried. The labor force grew by 421,000 and participation rose to 61.9 percent from 61.8. Two figures in the same report run the other way and are printed with the rest: the number working part time for economic reasons rose by 339,000 to 4.8 million, and long-term unemployment stands at 2.0 million, 27.6 percent of all unemployed, up from about 1.1 million in 2023. The private ADP report, already in at 86,000, which the overnight edition printed as the morning’s advance bearing, pointed the right way and understated the official figure by half.

The consumers in the same morning’s second report are less cheerful than the payrolls, and the survey predates the election. The University of Michigan’s preliminary November sentiment index rose to 51.0 from October’s final 48.0, against expectations of 47.5 to 48, per Dow Jones Newswires’ account: current conditions at 51.0, up from 46.7, expectations at 50.9, up from 48.8, and one-year inflation expectations down to 4.3 percent from 4.7. The interviews ran from October 20 to November 2 and closed before Tuesday’s results were known; the final November reading, with post-election interviews in it, comes later in the month. The index stands near its record low of 44.8, set in May. The two reports together are the morning’s economic whole: the hiring is stronger than anyone forecast, and the households being hired remain, by their own account, gloomy.

The Markets’ Reading at Noon: The Chips Bounce, the Dow Does Not

New York opened in the split the futures had promised, and the first hour widened the technology side of it. At 9:36 a.m. the Nasdaq Composite was up 1.2 percent at 24,601.93 and the S&P 500 up 0.38 percent at 7,381.99, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 449.65 points, or 0.87 percent, at 51,073.41, in the market account filed above. By 10:01 the bounce had broadened inside the same split: the Nasdaq up 1.7 percent at 24,732.09, the S&P 500 up 0.9 percent at 7,421.33, and the Dow’s loss pared to 127.38 points, or 0.2 percent. The early-session wrap, in quotes timed 15:42 GMT—10:42 a.m. ET—runs the same order an hour into the session: the Nasdaq 100 up 1.57 percent at 27,046.81, the Nasdaq Composite up 1.36 percent at 24,644.52, the S&P 500 up 0.74 percent at 7,408.36, and the Dow down 0.06 percent at 51,489.99, with information technology leading the S&P’s sectors at up 1.57 percent and consumer staples last, down 0.70 percent. Nvidia rose about 6 percent in early trading, and the semiconductor fund that fell by double digits on Thursday rose about 6.5 percent. The volatility index fell about 15 percent to 23.9 in one morning account. These are snapshots an hour into a session, printed as snapshots; Thursday’s closes stand beneath them, and what the bounce is worth belongs to the close.

Europe did not get the bounce, and its midday is the session’s plainest contrast. Reuters’ European file had the STOXX 600 down 1 percent at 648.83 by 0919 GMT, its gains for the week wiped out, with media, health care, and personal and household goods each down more than 2 percent and Teleperformance down 18 percent on a cut outlook. The London midday account, at 1219 GMT, runs the fall deeper: the STOXX 600 down 1.76 percent at 643, Germany down 2.44 percent, the United Kingdom down 2.21 percent, France down 1.76 percent, Italy down 1.23 percent, and Spain down 1.25 percent. A third account puts the STOXX 600 down 1.6 percent at 644.72 at its low. The three readings were taken at three hours of one falling session and are printed as a range, 1.0 to 1.76 percent. The shelter the overnight edition noted—Europe’s smaller share of the AI trade—held in degree and not in direction: the fall is a fraction of Tokyo’s 6 percent and Seoul’s 6 percent, and it is a fall, on the day the American technology shares themselves were recovering.

The Rate Reading: Three in Four for December

The payrolls moved the rate file further than the stock file. The ten-year Treasury yield rose about 3 to 4 basis points on the report, to 4.87–4.88 percent, and the dollar index rose 0.62 percent to about 102.22 in the post-report account. The CME FedWatch probability of a 25-basis-point increase at the Federal Reserve’s December 8–9 meeting rose to 76.8 percent after the release, from above 66 percent on Thursday, per the yields account carrying the CNBC reading and the jobs-and-rates account; a later state of the same tool runs at about 77 percent. The Fed’s range stands at 3.75 to 4.00 percent, held on October 28 by 10–2, with Governor Cook and Cleveland’s President Hammack preferring an increase. The next bearing is printed on the calendar: October consumer prices on Tuesday, November 10, and the November payrolls on December 4. Two Fed officials speak this afternoon, after this edition collects; their words belong to the Evening Watch.

Gold fell on the same figures, for the second session in a row. Spot gold stood at $4,048.97 an ounce at 0124 ET, down 1 percent, before the report, and at $4,047.10 after it, down 1 percent in the Reuters figures carried in the precious-metals update, with silver edging higher; the post-report account above runs gold at about $4,050, down 1.20 percent, with the dollar and yields up. The metal stands about 4 to 4.5 percent higher on the week even after two falling sessions, below Thursday’s two-week high of $4,146. The accounts give one reason in both directions: a labor market this firm gives the central bank room to raise rates, and higher rates are the weather gold does not like.

Oil Seesaws: Over a Hundred Before Breakfast, Under It by the London Morning

Brent crossed $100 for the second morning in a row and, for the second morning, did not hold it. The overnight states stand as Edition No. 10 printed them: $99.58 at 0504 GMT and $99.90 at 0730 GMT. A Mumbai account of the Asian morning puts Brent at $100.30, up 2 percent, at 0439 GMT in its figures, with West Texas Intermediate at $91.80. The later states run down. Dow Jones Newswires’ update, timed 0602 ET, has front-month Brent down 0.7 percent at $97.59 and West Texas Intermediate down 0.5 percent at $89.98. Reuters’ London file has January Brent down 74 cents, or 0.8 percent, at $97.55 by 0826 GMT, and West Texas Intermediate down 73 cents at $89.79. Thursday’s settlement stands beneath all of it: Brent $98.29, West Texas Intermediate $90.52.

The week’s bearing is where the files disagree, and the desk prints the disagreement. The London Reuters file puts Brent on track for a fall of 16 percent on the week—its steepest weekly percentage fall since the start of the pandemic, and its biggest in absolute terms in data back to 1988—with West Texas Intermediate down more than 13 percent. The Asian and overnight files put both benchmarks at about 12 percent on the week. The difference is the contract and the hour each file measures from, and it is printed rather than resolved. What no file disputes is the cargo in the price: de-escalation hopes after the election pulling down, tanker attacks at a near-record pace in the British agency’s count holding a floor, flows through the strait under 60 percent of capacity, and JPMorgan’s surplus estimate—supply ahead of demand by 1.1 million barrels a day in September and 1.4 million in October—standing against the rebound. Saudi Aramco on Thursday cut the December price of its Arab Light crude to Asia by $2 a barrel, per the Dow Jones update, the sellers’ own reading of the same market.

The Count at Noon: Mississippi Widens, Colorado Stands, Nothing Is Called

No race was called in the morning, in either chamber, in any state—the third morning running that sentence has led this section. The Senate stands at 54 seats for the Democrats and 44 for the Republicans, with Alaska and Mississippi uncalled in the Associated Press Senate file, which now lists Mississippi at 100 percent of precincts reporting and Alaska at 73.95 percent. The House moved at the edges. The wire’s national tracker in its latest state shows 249 seats won by the Democrats and 12 led, against 156 won and 18 led for the Republicans. The live results file, in its update of November 6 at 09:56 CET, runs the called figure higher: 253 House seats called for the Democrats and 157 for the Republicans, with 25 still uncalled. A third tally, updated at 3:55 a.m. EST, runs it higher still: 254 called for the Democrats and 160 for the Republicans, with 414 of 435 races called. Three methods, three hours, one chamber—and agreement, as on every morning of this count, on the outcome and on nothing smaller.

Mississippi’s margin widened in the newest tally, and the widening is the count’s one correction of substance. Decision Desk HQ’s update of November 6 at 03:29 EST, carried in the live results file, puts the Democrat, Scott Colom, at 467,233 votes and the incumbent Republican, Cindy Hyde-Smith, at 465,146—a lead of 2,087, with more than 95 percent of the estimated vote counted, the third candidate’s total revised down in the same update. The third tally above runs the same order narrower: Colom 466,877, Hyde-Smith 464,993, a lead of 1,884. The range this paper has printed for this race now runs from a few dozen votes in its earliest states to 2,087 in its newest, the leader the same in every state of it. The procedure stands as filed: affidavit identification due November 10, counties certify by November 13, the most votes wins, no automatic recount. Alaska stands exactly where it stood: the Democrat, Mary Peltola, ahead of the incumbent Republican, Dan Sullivan, by 637 first-choice votes, 102,962 to 102,325, with the ranked-choice tabulation set for November 18.

Colorado’s 4th District corrected its totals upward on both sides, and the margin corrected with them. The overnight edition, following the state file updated Thursday evening, carried the Democrat, Eileen Laubacher, at 184,103 votes and the incumbent Republican, Lauren Boebert, at 181,079—a margin of 3,024. The wire’s district file in its latest state carries both totals higher—Laubacher 184,624, Boebert 181,555, at 97.22 percent of precincts reporting and an estimated 97.3 percent of the vote—and the margin at 3,069, outside the roughly 920 votes that would require an automatic recount. The race is uncalled. What the morning added is the trailing campaign’s position: the account of the Boebert campaign’s statement records that the campaign is investigating what it calls unusual voting patterns, that its lawyer’s statement late Thursday insinuated a recount is forthcoming, and that under state law a recount at a margin above half a percent is paid for by the candidate who asks for it. The same account runs the lead at 2,927 in its own figures. The ballots that remain are signature cures and military and overseas ballots, due by November 12, with the counties finishing on November 13.

The Official Statements: A Big Agreement in Washington, No Details in Moscow

The president’s Thursday statement on Ukraine stands at noon with the Kremlin’s Friday answer beside it, and the two do not describe the same amount of knowledge. On Thursday, after meeting President Putin’s envoy Kirill Dmitriev at the White House, the president told reporters the sides were “very close” and, in the account of the meeting, that “it’s going to be a deal, it’s going to be a big deal” that could involve more than Ukraine and “all of Europe.” He gave no terms and no timeline, said he could not say what he and Dmitriev had discussed, and said he had not met the Ukrainian delegation that was also at the White House, for an event hosted by the first lady marking the six-day humanitarian ceasefire around Oleshky, which ran from October 27 to November 1 and has expired. On Friday the Kremlin spokesman, Dmitry Peskov, was asked about the agreement in Moscow. The account of his answer records it in three words—“there are no details”—and the rest of it: Dmitriev has not yet returned from the United States and has not reported to President Putin, and Russia has received no European ideas on security guarantees. American officials held discussions in Brussels the same day with Ukraine, NATO, and European partners on security guarantees, per the account of the meeting. Delegations from Washington, Moscow, and Kyiv are due in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11. Until one of the capitals puts terms on paper, the big agreement exists as the president’s description of it, with the other capital’s spokesman stating, on the record, that he has not been told what it is.

On Iran, no decision was announced by noon, and the strait file grew by claims. The president’s Thursday words stand where the overnight edition left them—a decision coming soon, no date named—and no announcement had followed by 1200. What arrived in the morning was Tehran’s. The Revolutionary Guards said on Friday that two more oil tankers caught fire after striking naval mines while crossing the strait by an unauthorized route, that both vessels had turned off their navigation and identification systems, that the strait remains closed until the United States meets Iran’s seven conditions, and that a naval electronic warfare unit took control of two uncrewed combat drones and landed them undamaged, per the agency account of the statement and the account carrying the statement’s text. No vessel was named, and no statement from the American military or any tanker operator appears in any file the desk took in the morning; the claims are filed as claims, beside the British agency’s standing count of at least five vessels reporting incidents since Sunday. The account of the president’s options runs them at four—a full resumption of the war, one large strike and an exit, continued pressure, or an interim deal on the Qatari track—with Kharg Island’s energy infrastructure named as the step Washington has not taken. The Qatari draft and Tehran’s seven conditions stand as the overnight edition printed them. Nothing was signed.

Washington’s own paper at noon is a deadline kept and a letter sent. Candidates for the House Republican leadership elections were required to declare by noon today, and no new name entered the field in the morning in any file on the shelf. The contest for minority leader stands as filed: Majority Leader Steve Scalise and Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, declared since Wednesday, with Speaker Mike Johnson not seeking the post; Majority Whip Tom Emmer seeking to remain whip, challenged by August Pfluger; the elections set for Tuesday, November 10. Mr. Scalise’s other act of the week reached print Friday: the account of his Thursday letter records that he asked Republican committee chairs to take inventory of the administration—to identify, in advance, the subjects the incoming majority’s investigations are expected to reach—while his own letter seeking the leadership calls for unity and for procedural disruption of the majority’s agenda. Mr. Jordan’s letter to his colleagues pitches him as battle-tested in the investigations to come. Both men are campaigning, in writing, for the job of leading the minority against the oversight the other letter is cataloguing. The House itself returns Monday.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. First, the Ukraine agreement: “very close” and “big” in the president’s Thursday words, “no details” in the Kremlin spokesman’s Friday words, with the envoy who carried whatever was discussed not yet home to report it—two capitals describing one meeting, and the distance between the descriptions is the fact. Second, the House at noon: 249 seats won in the wire’s tracker, 253 called in the live file’s morning check, 254 called in the third tally, with the uncalled running at 25 in one file and 21 in another. Third, Brent’s week: down about 12 percent in the Asian and overnight files, down 16 percent in the London file, the steepest since the pandemic in that file’s measure—one falling market read from two starting lines. Fourth, Mississippi: 1,884 in one tally and 2,087 in the newest, the lead widening in both directions of the comparison and the leader unchanged in every bearing this paper has ever printed for the race. Against the triangle, the load-bearing facts of the midday are single-valued: payrolls rose 165,000 and unemployment fell to 4.1 percent; September is revised to 60,000; the December hike probability stands above 76 percent; Brent trades under $100 and gold under $4,050; Europe is down between 1.0 and 1.76 percent at its midday; no race was called; two more tankers are claimed in the strait and none is confirmed; and the Abu Dhabi delegations meet on November 10, the same day the House conferences elect their leaders and Mississippi’s affidavit deadline falls. The session belongs to the close. The log proceeds to the evening.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. Thirty-five items.

Subjective
USA Today — robust October hiring defies expectations

Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, the Labor Department estimated on November 6, surpassing forecasters; September is revised to 60,000 from 29,000 and August to 186,000; average hourly earnings rose 14 cents to $38.00 and 3.1 percent over the year; participation inched up to 61.9 percent and unemployment ticked down to 4.1 percent; professional and business services added 70,000; long-term unemployment stands at 2 million; and most forecasters expect a quarter-point increase in December, per CME FedWatch.

Subjective
CNN — 165,000 jobs added, unemployment falls

The economy added 165,000 jobs in October and the unemployment rate fell to 4.1 percent from 4.2 percent, per the Bureau of Labor Statistics; the prior two months were revised up by a combined 84,000, August by 53,000 to 186,000 and September to 60,000; the consensus forecast called for 65,000 and 4.2 percent; the three-month average gain stands at 137,000; and professional and business services supplied the bulk of October’s gains, with 70,000.

Subjective
InvestingLive — October payrolls at 165,000 against 65,000 expected

The release in figures: nonfarm payrolls up 165,000 against 65,000 expected, the prior month revised to 60,000 from 29,000; unemployment at 4.1 percent against 4.2 expected, the unrounded rate at 4.141 percent against 4.1753 prior; private payrolls up 159,000 against 64,000 expected; and the note that the report makes a December increase more likely, with another report due before the December 9 meeting.

Subjective
Reuters, via 98.5 The River — job growth expected to pick up, in the preview

Washington, November 6, the preview filed before the release: payrolls likely increased by 65,000 in a Reuters survey, after September’s 29,000 gain was restricted by a calendar quirk; estimates ran from 35,000 to 125,000; the unemployment rate was expected unchanged at 4.2 percent, with a high probability it slipped to 4.1; and wages were forecast up 0.3 percent on the month and 2.9 percent on the year, the slowest annual pace in nearly five and a half years.

Subjective
Dow Jones Newswires, via Morningstar — consumer mood improved, and remained gloomy

The University of Michigan’s preliminary November sentiment index landed at 51, against 48 in October’s final reading and a Wall Street Journal survey expecting 47.5; the interviews ran October 20 to November 2 and wrapped up before the election results were known; the index hit its record low of 44.8 in May; and the survey’s director is quoted on the reading.

Subjective
Kitco — gold near $4,050 after sentiment rises to 51

The preliminary sentiment reading at 51 against a consensus of 48, the same as October’s final; the survey director’s sentence that sentiment ticked up about 6 percent in the preliminary read; the survey conducted October 20 to November 2, ending just before the midterm election; and gold trading near $4,050 an ounce in the same file.

Subjective
JBizNews — stocks open mixed after the jobs report

Wall Street opened mixed after the report: at 9:36 a.m. the Nasdaq Composite was up 1.2 percent at 24,601.93 and the S&P 500 up 0.38 percent at 7,381.99, while the Dow was down 449.65 points at 51,073.41; by 10:01 the Nasdaq was up 1.7 percent, the S&P 500 up 0.9 percent, and the Dow’s loss pared to 0.2 percent; Nvidia jumped about 6 percent early; the ten-year yield rose about 3 basis points to 4.87 percent; and the report’s sector detail—professional and business services 70,000, health care 42,000, transportation and warehousing 25,000, manufacturing 19,000, and 421,000 joining the labor force.

Subjective
The Edge — the early-session wrap, November 6

Quotes timed 15:42 GMT, about an hour into Friday’s session: four of five tracked indexes higher, the Nasdaq 100 up 1.57 percent at 27,046.81, the Nasdaq Composite up 1.36 percent at 24,644.52, the S&P 500 up 0.74 percent at 7,408.36, and the Dow down 0.06 percent at 51,489.99; information technology led the S&P’s sectors at up 1.57 percent and consumer staples fell furthest at 0.70 percent; CNBC’s account of investors buying back into chip stocks is cited; and the snapshots are stated not to be closes.

Subjective
CoinDesk — the live file, futures and the jobs beat

The Nasdaq up 2 percent a few minutes into Friday’s session, the semiconductor fund up 6.5 percent after its double-digit fall, and the S&P 500 up 1 percent with defensive names lower; the jobs gain of 165,000 topping the highest Wall Street forecast of 131,000 by 34,000; September revised to 60,000; Nasdaq 100 futures ahead 1.5 percent before the open while Dow futures fell about 1 percent; and Bitcoin near $75,800, little changed after the news.

Subjective
MarketSpeaker — yields rise, December hike bets rise

Employers added 165,000 jobs and the prior gains were revised up by a combined 84,000; an early CME FedWatch reading cited by CNBC put the December quarter-point hike odds above 76 percent, from more than 66 percent on Thursday; the Fed left its range at 3.75 to 4.00 percent on October 28 by 10–2, with Governor Cook and President Hammack preferring an increase; the next meeting is December 8–9, and a quarter point would take the range to 4.00–4.25 percent; and the next inflation release is due Tuesday, November 10.

Subjective
Invezz — 165,000 jobs, December bets grow

Nonfarm payrolls increased by a seasonally adjusted 165,000 in October; traders raised the probability of a quarter-point increase at the December 8–9 meeting to 76.8 percent, per CME FedWatch; the indicator pointed to one additional increase after that meeting, with expectations for further 2027 hikes easing; an analyst’s view that the Fed will hike 25 basis points in December and probably two to three more times in the first half of 2027 is quoted; and next Tuesday’s inflation report is named as the next clue.

Subjective
Reuters, via Devdiscourse — European shares fall as the rout gathers pace

Friday in Europe: the STOXX 600 dropped 1 percent to 648.83 by 0919 GMT, wiping out its gains for the week; media, health care, and personal and household goods led declines at over 2 percent each; Teleperformance fell 18 percent after cutting its outlook; clean energy shares rose, with Orsted up 2.7 percent and Nordex up 1.7 percent, and EDP added 1.6 percent on raised guidance; airlines rose, IAG up 2 percent, Lufthansa up 2.4 percent, and Air France-KLM up 5 percent; and the index’s smaller AI exposure is stated as its relative shelter.

Subjective
Financial News, via LSE — Europe at midday, losses extend

European markets at midday on Friday: the Stoxx 600 down 1.76 percent at 643 at 1219 GMT, with Germany down 2.44 percent, the United Kingdom down 2.21 percent, France down 1.76 percent, Italy down 1.23 percent, and Spain down 1.25 percent; more than $3.2 trillion wiped from American equity values in Thursday’s session, in the file’s figure; the chipmakers and related industries named as gainers on the day against the fall; and Teleperformance down on its lowered revenue outlook, with IAG lower on its third-quarter profit.

Subjective
Finimize — Europe’s stocks slid as AI jitters spread

The STOXX Europe 600 fell 1.6 percent to 644.72, wiping out the week’s gains and leaving the index slightly lower on the week; Europe had looked steadier than the United States and parts of Asia because the benchmark holds fewer mega-cap AI leaders, and the drop showed how quickly the nerves travel; Teleperformance sank 18 percent on its cut outlook; and the Democrat-led Congress’s possible limits on data-center spending are named as one fresh worry.

Subjective
Reuters, via 98.5 The River — oil set for a sharp weekly drop, the London state

London, November 6: after early gains in a see-saw session, January Brent was down 74 cents, or 0.8 percent, at $97.55 a barrel by 0826 GMT, and West Texas Intermediate was down 73 cents at $89.79; Brent is on track for a 16 percent fall on the week, its steepest weekly percentage fall since the start of the pandemic and its biggest in absolute terms in data back to 1988, with West Texas Intermediate set for more than 13 percent; Wednesday’s 8 percent fall on the election result is recorded; and the British agency’s data show attacks on oil-carrying ships still running at close to record pace.

Subjective
Dow Jones Newswires, via Morningstar — oil slides below $100

Front-month Brent fell 0.7 percent to $97.59 a barrel and West Texas Intermediate futures fell 0.5 percent to $89.98 on Friday, in the update timed 06:02 ET, both on track for weekly losses of nearly 14 percent; prices volatile since the week’s selloff on hopes of a diplomatic resolution; attacks on shipping in the strait and the threat to Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea lane stated as the risks to a recovery in Gulf exports; Saudi Aramco’s $2 cut to the December price of Arab Light to Asia; and JPMorgan’s surplus estimates of 1.1 million barrels a day in September and 1.4 million in October.

Subjective
FinanceFeeds — Brent at $99.90 on Friday morning

Updated November 6 at 07:30 GMT, carrying CNBC’s figures: Brent up 1.67 percent to $99.90 a barrel and West Texas Intermediate up 1.43 percent to $91.69, with a second account putting Brent at $100.30 at 0439 GMT; Brent still heading for a weekly loss of about 12 percent; the reference levels at $93.50 below and $103.60 above; Iran’s three more reported tanker attacks on Thursday and the near-record rate in the British agency’s data; flows through the strait at less than 60 percent of capacity; and the jobs report named as the day’s demand question.

Subjective
HDFC Sky, carrying OilPrice — Brent reclaims $100 in the Asian morning
