Brent gained 2 percent to $100.30 a barrel and West Texas Intermediate advanced 1.5 percent to $91.80, extending the recovery for a second session on fresh attacks on commercial vessels; both benchmarks remained on course for weekly losses of around 12 percent, Brent 12 percent and West Texas Intermediate 12.1 percent; Iran reported three more tankers attacked on Thursday, and the British agency’s data show incidents at close to record levels; flows through the strait run at less than 60 percent of capacity; and the tug-of-war between de-escalation expectations and supply risk is stated as the market’s position.

Subjective
FXStreet — gold falls as the strong payrolls lift the dollar

Gold trades around $4,050, down 1.20 percent on the day, after climbing to a two-week high of $4,146 on Thursday; the economy added 165,000 jobs against a 65,000 forecast and September was revised to 60,000, with unemployment down to 4.1 percent; the stronger figures strengthen the case for a December increase, which weighs on a metal that pays no yield; the dollar index trades around 102.22, up 0.62 percent; the ten-year yield rose 4 basis points to 4.88 percent; and West Texas Intermediate is down around 12 percent on the week in the same file.

Subjective
Reuters figures, via Limitless Metals — gold pulls back, silver holds

Spot gold at $4,047.10 an ounce, down 1 percent, following the stronger-than-expected employment data, with the dollar and Treasury yields higher; silver edged higher; gold remained up approximately 4.5 percent for the week; and the figures are stated to be intraday observations from the November 6 Reuters update, not closing prices.

Subjective
Associated Press — Senate, every state

The Senate file in its latest state: 35 races listed, Alaska too early to call at 73.95 percent of precincts reporting and Mississippi too early to call at 100 percent of precincts reporting, and the remaining races called state by state.

Subjective
Associated Press — House, national balance of power

The House tracker in its latest state: 249 seats won by the Democrats and 12 led, against 156 won and 18 led for the Republicans, across all 435 districts, with 218 needed for a majority; the national vote totals by party are carried in the same file.

Subjective
Votendi — the live results file, November 6 update

The update of November 6 at 09:56 CET: 253 House seats called for the Democrats and 157 for the Republicans, with 25 still uncalled, in the Associated Press results published by The Guardian and the decision desk’s national display; the Senate at 54 seats for the Democrats and 44 for the Republicans, Alaska and Mississippi uncalled; Mississippi at 467,233 votes for Colom and 465,146 for Hyde-Smith, a lead of 2,087, in the decision desk’s update of November 6 at 03:29 EST, with the third candidate’s total revised down; and Alaska’s first-choice totals unchanged at 102,962 to 102,325, a lead of 637.

Subjective
Poliwave — the Senate live map, November 6

Updated November 6 at 3:55 a.m. EST: 33 of 35 Senate races called, Alaska and Mississippi counting; the House at 414 of 435 races called, 254 for the Democrats and 160 for the Republicans, with 8 Democratic-led and 13 Republican-led races still counting; Mississippi at 466,877 for Colom and 464,993 for Hyde-Smith; and Alaska’s first choices at 102,962 for Peltola, with the ranked-choice count noted.

Subjective
Associated Press — Colorado’s 4th District

Laubacher 184,624, Boebert 181,555, with 97.22 percent of precincts reporting and an estimated 97.3 percent of the vote in the latest state of the count. The race is labeled too early to call.

Subjective
NewsViews — the Boebert campaign investigates, and speaks of a recount

The campaign of Representative Lauren Boebert says it is investigating unusual voting patterns in Colorado’s 4th District while the counting continues and she trails; her lawyer’s statement late Thursday insinuated a recount would be forthcoming, and by law she would pay for one if the margin is larger than half a percent; the lead is put at 2,927 in the file’s figures, well outside the automatic-recount threshold of 921 votes; an estimated 97 percent of votes had been counted with about 12,000 outstanding in the NBC News estimate at 7:30 a.m. ET Friday; and Weld County’s clerk states the county is done counting except cures and forwarded ballots.

Subjective
Harava News — the president says a Ukraine deal is close

On November 5 the president said a deal to end Russia’s war against Ukraine was close after he met the Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev, gave no details, and said he had not met the Ukrainian delegation visiting Washington; the agreement could cover more than Ukraine and involve Europe, he said; Dmitriev had appeared at a White House event hosted by the first lady, where Russian and Ukrainian representatives discussed the six-day ceasefire around Oleshky that expired November 1; American officials held discussions in Brussels with Ukraine, NATO, and European partners on security guarantees the same day; and talks mediated by the United States are scheduled in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11.

Subjective
Silent Dossier — the Kremlin says it has no details

On Friday, November 6, the Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was asked about the agreement the president announced the evening before and answered that there are no details; Dmitriev has not yet returned or reported to President Putin, he said; Russia has received no European ideas on security guarantees; the president’s Thursday words are quoted—“it’s going to be a big agreement” and it might involve all of Europe—with his statement that he could not say what he discussed with Dmitriev; and delegations from Washington, Moscow, and Kyiv are due in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11.

Subjective
Public Radio East — the first lady’s Oleshky meeting

The first lady hosted a meeting between Russian and Ukrainian officials at the White House to recognize the temporary ceasefire in southeastern Ukraine; the six-day pause around the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky enabled humanitarian aid to reach the city and hundreds of residents to be evacuated, and it expired on Sunday; the Russian envoy thanked the first lady; the president also met the envoy and told reporters the sides were close to a deal; and the event comes days before a new round of talks in Abu Dhabi.

Subjective
AsiaPost, carrying the agencies — two tankers caught fire, the Guards say

Tehran, November 6: the Revolutionary Guards said two oil tankers seeking to transit the strait through an unauthorized route caught fire after hitting naval mines, both vessels having turned off their navigation and identification systems; the strait remains closed and no change will occur unless the United States meets Iran’s seven conditions; Thursday’s earlier claim of three vessels, including two supertankers, catching fire on the same route is recorded; and a naval electronic warfare unit took control of two uncrewed combat drones and landed them unharmed, the Guards said.

Subjective
Nation Press — tankers ablaze at Hormuz after hitting mines

The Guards announced on Friday, November 6, that two oil tankers attempting the strait through an unauthorized route caught fire after striking naval mines, the vessels’ navigation and identification systems disabled; the statement, published on the Guards’ own outlet, accuses the American military of supporting the crossing and warns its forces against compelling vessels across the mined corridor; the strait stays closed until Washington meets seven conditions, the specific terms not detailed in the statement; the seizure of two drones is claimed in the same report; and the claims are stated not to have been independently verified, with no statement from the American military or the tanker operators at the time of publication.

Subjective
OilPrice — the Iran strategy at a crossroads

The president’s four paths after the midterm defeat are set out: a full resumption of the war; one large strike, then an exit, with the underground site at Pickaxe Mountain named as a possible target; continued pressure; and an interim deal on the Qatari track resembling June’s collapsed memorandum, with Iran offering to reopen the strait within two days if its seven conditions are met; Kharg Island’s energy infrastructure is named as the step Washington has not taken, the blockade having driven Iranian exports to near zero; reports from late October that allies were warned of a short, intense campaign after the elections are recorded; and the president’s November 4 answer on when the war ends is quoted: “Whenever I want it to.”

Subjective
MEAWW — Scalise tells his chairs to take inventory

Majority Leader Steve Scalise urged Republican committee chairs on Thursday, November 5, to identify potential targets across the administration and prepare for the investigations the incoming majority is expected to launch; his bid for minority leader, announced Wednesday, calls for unity, strategic disruption of the majority’s agenda by procedural tools, and continued wins on appropriations, health care, immigration, and superintelligence; Representative Jim Jordan, who has reached his term limit as Judiciary chairman, is seeking the same post and argues his investigations experience suits him for it; and Democratic criticism of the inventory letter is recorded in the same file.

Subjective
Wikipedia — the 2026 House Republican Conference leadership election

The election set for November 10, 2026, with representatives required to declare by November 6: Speaker Johnson declined for minority leader; Scalise and Jordan declared, from Louisiana’s 1st district and Ohio’s 4th; Whip Emmer seeking re-election and challenged by Pfluger of Texas’s 11th; Conference Chair McClain seeking re-election; and the campaign-arm chair’s race open after the incumbent lost his North Carolina seat.

Subjective
The Bilig — the daily brief, November 6

The day in one file: the AI sell-off giving Wall Street its worst day since April 2025 and spreading across Asia; the president warning Iran could face further destruction and saying a decision was coming, after meeting his national security team; the Guards’ claim to have shot down two American drones, in the brief’s words; Iranian forces saying at least five tankers and a tugboat caught fire on Thursday, with two more tankers said to have hit mines on Friday, the claims not independently confirmed; Brent settled at $98.29 on Thursday and West Texas Intermediate at $90.52; the president’s Thursday statement that a Russia-Ukraine settlement was close, after meeting the Russian envoy at the White House; and the Bank of England’s increase to 4 percent.
items.summary: The midday file for November 6, 2026: October payrolls at 165,000 against a 59,000 consensus and unemployment at 4.1 percent, the Nasdaq bouncing an hour into the session, Europe down at its midday, Brent seesawing under $100, Mississippi's margin wider at 2,087, Colorado's 4th at 3,069, the Kremlin answering the president's big agreement with no details, and two more tankers claimed in the strait. Collected at 1200.

items.title: The Offer and the Answer: What the Ballot Box Did to the Tax Base
items.content_html:
Breaking Report

The Infrastructure File — The Tax Base and the Ballot

Objective

The Offer and the Answer: What the Ballot Box Did to the Tax Base

On November 3 the voters limited the data-center buildout in forty of forty-one local decisions. The offers those decisions answered are also in the record: the tax revenue projected, the jobs counted, and the one county that said yes for twenty-five years and now collects $1.2 billion a year. The desk files the two records side by side.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1145 ET, Friday, November 6, 2026.

The News in the File

Ballotpedia records 41 local ballot measures on data-center policy in ten states, tallied after the election: on 28 a yes vote would limit development through bans or moratoriums, and on 13 a yes vote would facilitate it. Voters approved 27 of the limiting measures and defeated all 13 of the facilitating ones. The single exception is Harwood, North Dakota, which defeated a measure adding review requirements to industrial projects.

Ohio held twenty-one of the forty-one measures in eighteen municipalities, and the margins were not narrow. By the Cincinnati Enquirer’s accounting, eleven municipalities passed outright bans, among them Trenton, at 80 percent to 20 percent, and Sunbury, where a charter amendment banning facilities of 25 megawatts or more passed with 78.6 percent. In Perry, more than 87 percent approved financial-guarantee requirements on incentivized developers. In Wilmington, below, about 80 percent rejected each of four rezonings. Six measures decided earlier in 2026 had already run the same way: Canterbury, New Hampshire, prohibited data centers in March, 322 to 63; Monterey Park, California, in June, 10,388 to 1,372; Augusta Township, Michigan, overturned a rezoning in August, 2,314 to 269.

The ballot measures are the counted part of a larger record. Fortune counted at least 138 Ohio municipalities and townships with active moratoriums as of September 17; the National Conference of State Legislatures found lawmakers in at least 28 of the 38 states offering data-center tax incentives pursuing rollbacks this year; Data Center Watch counted some $68 billion of projects blocked or delayed in the second quarter of 2026 alone. What follows is the other half of the file: the fiscal record of the places doing the voting, the terms of the offers they answered, and the realized record of the places that answered the other way. Figures from adopted budgets and legislative audits are printed as record; figures from developers of unbuilt projects, as company figures.

The Offer, Measured

The most complete audit of what a data center offers a locality was made in Virginia, and its job count is modest. Industry representatives told the Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission, the General Assembly’s oversight arm, reporting on December 9, 2024, that a typical 250,000-square-foot data center employs approximately 50 full-time workers, about half of them contract workers. Construction is the larger employment event: a building takes twelve to eighteen months to raise, with approximately 1,500 workers on site at the peak, and the jobs tend to be high-paying. Statewide, the commission estimated the industry contributes 74,000 jobs and $9.1 billion in gross domestic product each year, most of the benefit deriving from construction. A Brookings study of counties receiving a first large data center found private employment up 4 to 5 percent over five to six years; estimates ignoring pre-existing trends overstate the effect by about three times.

The revenue side of the audit is larger than the jobs side, and varies by two orders of magnitude between localities. In the five Virginia localities with relatively mature data-center markets, data-center revenue ranged from less than 1 percent of total local revenue to 31 percent. The commission’s sentence on the geography of the benefit is printed as written: localities in economically distressed areas of the state could benefit from data centers through increased local tax revenue, but these localities could have difficulty attracting the industry. Against the revenue stand the incentives: states forgo more than $3 billion a year to data-center tax exemptions, by Good Jobs First’s estimate, and the commission put Virginia’s return on its own sales-tax exemption at about 48 cents recovered per dollar forgone.

Wilmington, Ohio: Four Votes on 546 Acres

Wilmington is a city of 12,802 people in Clinton County, in the farm country between Cincinnati and Columbus. Census figures (2020–2024 American Community Survey) put median household income at $57,199, against $80,734 nationally, and 17.5 percent of residents in poverty; Clinton County stands higher, at $70,407 and 11.9 percent. The city’s modern history has one large event in it. Its air park was the national sorting hub of Airborne Express and then of DHL; when DHL ended its United States domestic delivery service in 2009, the hub closed, at a loss the Greater Ohio Policy Center puts at 16,000 jobs in the area. Air cargo returned in time—Amazon Air operates at the air park today—and the population stands 138 above its 2020 count.

Two data-center rezonings reached Wilmington in 2026, and only one of them reached the voters. On September 3 the council, acting by emergency ordinances effective immediately and not subject to referendum under Ohio law, rezoned the 471-acre Cosler Farm on U.S. 68 for a proposed $4 billion Amazon Web Services campus of about 1.9 million square feet. Separately, the council rezoned four parcels, about 546 acres, from rural residential to light industrial for a project of Ardent, affiliated with TAC Data Centers; the four would have taken the city’s land zoned for data centers from about 500 acres to more than 1,000. A residents’ group collected 1,529 signatures in about twenty-five days and placed the four on the ballot. On November 3, each was rejected by about 80 percent of the voters; the first ordinance drew 739 in favor and 2,885 against, in the Wilmington News Journal’s county totals, unofficial pending certification. The four parcels remain rural residential. The emergency rezoning was not decided on November 3 and is not affected by the vote.

Three Michigan Townships

Augusta Township, in Washtenaw County southeast of Ann Arbor, is a farming community of 7,345 people, and its census figures are not a distressed place’s figures. The Census Bureau puts its median household income at $108,457, above its county’s $89,180. In July 2025 the board voted unanimously, against its own planning commission’s recommendation, to rezone 522 acres of farmland for a Thor Equities data center reported at $1 billion; officials pointed at the time to millions of dollars a year in new tax revenue for the township and its schools. Opponents needed 561 signatures to force a vote and turned in nearly twice that within about a month. On August 4, 2026, the voters overturned the rezoning, 2,314 to 269. Residents have since filed petitions to recall the board members who approved it.

Delhi Township, south of Lansing, answered an offer that had not yet become an application. The township has 28,431 people, a median household income of $90,437, per the Census Bureau’s tables, and, by the Lansing State Journal’s account, annual tax revenue of $23 million; a twelve-month moratorium adopted in April runs to April 2027. On October 27 the Lansing Economic Area Partnership and Lighthouse Sustainability, a Colorado developer, announced a proposed 700-megawatt data center on 423 acres, an investment stated above $10 billion, without prior consultation with the township, by the manager’s statement. The sponsors’ projections were township tax revenue more than tripling, $23 million a year to $76 million, with $16 million a year added to the Holt and Mason schools, a $20 million community fund, and a no-cost residential solar program. On October 28 the township withdrew from the partnership. On October 30, three days after the announcement, the board voted 6 to 0 to record its opposition to any data center development in the township. No application had been filed.

Saline Township, twenty miles south of Augusta, said no and was answered in court. It is a farming community of about 2,375 people; a policy study of the case puts its annual budget at roughly $1 million. Related Digital proposed a multi-building campus there for Oracle and OpenAI on about 575 acres. On September 10, 2025, the board voted 4 to 1 to deny the rezoning; the developer sued two days later; on October 15 a consent judgment rezoned the site and bound the township to approve a twelve-year, 50 percent tax abatement whose final value awaits the State Tax Commission. The settlement’s tax-exemption form lists $1.31 billion of real property and $3.5 billion of equipment, $4.81 billion in all. The company’s 2026 statements value the project above $43 billion and put the resulting tax revenue, after the abatement, at about $147 million a year to county, schools, and township—well north of $150 million a year for the better part of two decades, in Oracle’s release—with more than 2,500 union construction jobs and about 450 permanent on-site jobs, all company figures. Construction began June 1, 2026; by late September the company reported one million union craft hours worked. The township’s share, the company states, is more than 2,000 times what the land would have yielded as farmland.

The Places That Said Yes

Pike County, Ohio, holds the poorest census figures in this file, and it signed the largest agreement in it. The county, in the Appalachian foothills, has 27,061 people, 27 below its 2020 count; the Census Bureau puts median household income at $52,736 and 19.1 percent of residents in poverty. Its largest site is the decommissioned Portsmouth Gaseous Diffusion Plant, whose cleanup has employed the county for a generation. On August 17, 2026, SB Energy, OpenAI, and Nvidia announced the PORTS-Pike Technology Campus on that ground: SB Energy will build, own, and operate the campus and lease approximately eight gigawatts of capacity to OpenAI for twenty years, with Nvidia the exclusive supplier of the computing infrastructure and $1.5 billion invested in SB Energy. The companies’ stated terms are 35,000 construction jobs across a six-year buildout through 2032 and 2,500 long-term operating jobs, capacity phased from 2028, the developer paying the full cost of the grid upgrades required, at least $4.2 billion of regional grid infrastructure built with AEP Ohio, and community funds of $40 million from each company. Every figure in this paragraph is a company projection attached to an agreement signed in August. Pike County’s permanent-jobs figure, 2,500 across eight gigawatts, stands beside the Virginia auditors’ figure for one typical facility, about fifty; the difference is the difference between a campus and a building.

Massena, New York, voted the other way on the only question put to it, by three votes to two. The town, on the St. Lawrence River, has 12,058 people; the Census Bureau puts its median household income at $54,595 and its poverty rate at 23.1 percent, the highest in this file. Its industrial ground is the former Alcoa East and Reynolds Metals site, shuttered aluminum works. North Country Colocation Services, an affiliate of the New York Digital Investment Group, proposes a 1.5-million-square-foot data center there; the company states about 200 permanent jobs, and construction estimates run from 1,800 to 2,500 workers over about two years. On September 16 the town board voted 3 to 2 against a six-month moratorium; the proposal proceeds without the pause its opponents petitioned for. Over the project stands a state question: the governor’s July 14 executive order paused state environmental permits for large data centers for up to a year; the developer states the project is exempt, and state officials have not confirmed it.

In Hermantown, Minnesota, the terms changed before the answer did. On October 30, after two meetings halted by protests and four hours of testimony running mostly against the project, the city council voted unanimously to approve a Google campus of about 1.7 million square feet and some 500 megawatts of demand. Before the vote, Google had withdrawn a request for up to $80 million in property tax abatements, reduced the project from four buildings to three, and signed a decommissioning agreement valued at $210 million. The Hermantown and Delhi sequences closed in the same week. In Delhi, the answer came three days after an announcement and before any application. In Hermantown, it came after the abatement request was withdrawn.

Loudoun County: The Realized Record

One county in the record has run the experiment to completion, and its figures are budget figures, not projections. Loudoun County, Virginia, the largest data-center market in the world, has 449,749 people, up from 312,311 in 2010; the Census Bureau puts its median household income at $181,765, the highest county figure in the nation, and its poverty rate at 4.3 percent. In fiscal 2026, by the county’s own published figures, data centers generated $1.2 billion in real and personal property tax revenue, 39 percent of the county’s overall budget. The adopted fiscal 2027 budget projects about $1.3 billion, roughly 45 percent of local tax revenue and 38 percent of the general fund by budget analyses; of the total, about $417 million is real property tax and about $879 million is personal property tax on the equipment inside the buildings, taxed at $4.15 per $100 of value. The county has cut its homeowner real property rate every year for ten years, $1.145 per $100 in 2016 to $0.805 in 2026, and attributes the cuts to the data-center revenue; its budget office states that without the industry the rate would likely exceed one dollar. In 2023 the county created a Revenue Stabilization Fund, against the stated risk that data-center revenue falls short of the budget built on it.

The county that collects the revenue has also begun, in the same years, to close the door it opened. On March 18, 2025, the Board of Supervisors voted 7 to 2 to end by-right development; new projects require a special exception. In September 2026 the board voted 7 to 1 to 1 to draft a twelve-month pause on new data-center and substation applications. The two halves of the national record meet in these figures and are printed together, without a sentence between them: Loudoun County’s median household income is $181,765, and it is drafting a pause. Wilmington’s median household income is $57,199, its poverty rate is 17.5 percent, and it voted four times, by about four to one, to keep 546 acres in rural residential zoning. Massena’s poverty rate is 23.1 percent, and its board voted 3 to 2 to let a proposal proceed. Pike County’s poverty rate is 19.1 percent, and its ground holds a signed agreement for eight gigawatts. The log proceeds to the Evening Watch.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. The national count carries one: Ballotpedia’s verified list holds 41 measures decided on November 3, another tracker lists 47 for the same day, the inclusion rules separating the lists are not published, and the desk prints Ballotpedia’s 41 with the range noted. The DHL figure carries one: the Greater Ohio Policy Center puts the 2009 loss at 16,000 jobs in the area, while county accounts describe thousands eliminated; the desk prints the policy center’s figure as its figure. Saline Township carries the widest triangle in the file: the settlement’s filing values the project at $4.81 billion, the company’s 2026 statements above $43 billion, the $147 million annual tax figure is the company’s arithmetic, the abatement it assumes has not received its final value from the State Tax Commission, and the division of the revenue among county, schools, and township has not been published. Two categories of number run through this report and are not interchangeable: Delhi’s $76 million and Pike County’s 35,000 construction jobs are sponsor projections for unbuilt projects, the second stated across a six-year buildout without a statement of whether it counts positions or job-years; Loudoun’s $1.2 billion is an adopted budget’s accounting of money collected. The Ohio results are unofficial until the county boards certify them. Against the triangle, the single-valued facts stand: the votes were cast as counted above; the census figures are the bureau’s; the Virginia audit’s typical facility employs about fifty people; and in every locality in this file, the offer and the answer are both matters of public record.

The Clippings Filed With This Report

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only part of this file stamped objective. Fourteen items.

Subjective
Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission—Data Centers in Virginia

The General Assembly’s audit of the industry, dated December 9, 2024: a typical 250,000-square-foot facility employs about fifty full-time workers, about half of them contractors; construction peaks near 1,500 workers per building over twelve to eighteen months; the industry contributes an estimated 74,000 jobs and $9.1 billion in gross domestic product statewide, mostly from construction; in five mature localities data-center revenue ran from under 1 percent to 31 percent of total local revenue; and distressed localities could benefit from the tax revenue but could have difficulty attracting the industry.

Subjective
Ballotpedia News — the pre-election tally of the measures

The tracker’s account before the vote: 41 local measures in ten states on November 3, twenty-eight of them limiting development if approved and thirteen facilitating it; six measures decided earlier in 2026, each classified as an outcome favoring limits; and thirty-eight states offering tax incentives for data centers as of April 2026. The report’s count of forty of forty-one is this file’s post-election tally.

Subjective
Route Fifty — voters reject data centers in local initiatives

The election account of the local votes: more than forty measures across ten states, the opponents of data-center development successful in virtually all of them, Ohio carrying the most initiatives, some votes advisory rather than binding, and a single locality, Harwood, North Dakota, where the outcome favored development.

Subjective
Cincinnati Enquirer — Ohioans pass data center bans and restrictions

The state paper’s town-by-town results: eleven municipalities passing bans on construction, among them Hubbard, Sunbury, Pataskala, Urbana, Defiance, Upper Sandusky, Piqua, Granville, Conneaut, Oregon, and Trenton; other municipalities passing restrictions; Wilmington rejecting rezoning in four referendums by about 80 percent; and Perry approving financial guarantees from developers. All Ohio results unofficial until certification.

Subjective
U.S. Census Bureau — QuickFacts, Wilmington city and Clinton County, Ohio

The bureau’s tables for the city and its county: Wilmington population 12,802, median household income $57,199, poverty 17.5 percent; Clinton County median household income $70,407 and poverty 11.9 percent; income and poverty from the 2020–2024 American Community Survey, population estimated at July 1, 2025.

Subjective
Greater Ohio Policy Center — Wilmington, the logistics center

The policy center’s profile of the city: the airport taken over in the Second World War, developed as an air park, and made a national sorting hub by Airborne Express and then DHL; the 2009 end of DHL’s domestic service and the closure of the Wilmington facility, with the loss put at 16,000 jobs in the area; the Green Enterprise Zone the city adopted in response; and the return of air cargo, with the air park again the highest-volume cargo airport in Ohio.

Subjective
Data Catalyst Institute — the referendum belt

The institute’s study of the year’s local votes: a belt of rural towns, most of which have never hosted a data center, deciding the buildout at the ballot box; some $68 billion of projects blocked or delayed in the second quarter of 2026; and the Augusta Township sequence in full—the board’s unanimous rezoning of 522 acres for a $1 billion project against its planning commission’s recommendation, the officials’ case of millions a year in tax revenue, the petition drive at nearly twice the required signatures, and the August vote overturning the rezoning by about nine to one.

Subjective
Lansing State Journal — Delhi Township rejects all data centers

The capital city paper’s account of the October 30 vote: trustees unanimous, 6 to 0, in a resolution opposing any data center development and calling on the partnership and the developer to cease their efforts; the $10 billion, 700-megawatt, 423-acre proposal announced three days earlier; the township’s moratorium to April 2027; and the sponsors’ figures—township tax revenue more than tripling from $23 million to $76 million a year, $16 million more for the Holt and Mason schools, and a $20 million community fund.

Subjective
The Saline Township case file — denial, suit, and consent judgment

A case analysis of the township that said no and was sued: the board’s 4 to 1 denial of September 10, 2025; the developer’s suit two days later; the consent judgment of October 15, 2025, rezoning the site and binding the township to a twelve-year, 50 percent abatement; the settlement filing’s $4.81 billion of listed property against the company’s later $43 billion figure; and the company’s claim of about $147 million a year in tax revenue after abatement, with the division among the taxing units unpublished. Company claims are labeled as claims throughout the file.

Subjective
Oracle — construction begins at the Saline Township campus

The operator’s announcement of the June 1, 2026, groundbreaking: the campus described as the largest economic investment in Michigan’s history; tax revenues stated in the billions over the better part of two decades, averaging well north of $150 million a year, with the township receiving almost half the benefit and more than 2,000 times what the land would have yielded as farmland; a first-in-the-nation project labor agreement; and the project paying the full cost of the electricity infrastructure it requires. The figures are the company’s projections, and the report prints them as such.

Subjective
OpenAI — the PORTS-Pike agreement, Pike County, Ohio

The customer’s statement of the August agreement: approximately eight gigawatts of capacity at the former Portsmouth enrichment site, built and operated by SB Energy under a twenty-year lease; 35,000 construction jobs projected across the six-year buildout and 2,500 long-term operating jobs; the project paying its own energy and infrastructure costs; a $40 million community grant fund added to SB Energy’s $40 million; and annual public reporting on hiring, water, and energy promised. All figures are the companies’ projections for capacity arriving from 2028.

Subjective
ClickNNY — Massena board rejects a moratorium

The North Country account of the September 16 vote: the town board 3 to 2 against a six-month moratorium while a 1.5-million-square-foot facility is proposed for the former Alcoa East and Reynolds site; the company’s figure of about 200 permanent jobs and construction estimates of 1,800 to 2,500 workers; the governor’s statewide pause on environmental permits for large data centers; and the developer’s position that the project is exempt from the pause, unconfirmed by state officials.

Subjective
Charged Up Pro — voters, councils, and townships redraw the map

A trade roundup of the season’s local decisions: the Delhi Township sequence, from announcement without consultation to the 6 to 0 vote and the severed partnership; Hermantown’s unanimous approval of the Google campus after the company dropped a request for up to $80 million in tax breaks, cut a building, and signed a $210 million decommissioning agreement; and the National Conference of State Legislatures’ finding that lawmakers in at least 28 of 38 incentive states pursued rollbacks this year.

Subjective
Polimetrics — Loudoun County’s $1.3 billion

An analysis of Loudoun County’s adopted fiscal 2027 budget: about $1.3 billion of projected data-center revenue, roughly 45 percent of local tax revenue, divided between about $417 million of real property tax and about $879 million of personal property tax on equipment at $4.15 per $100; the homeowner rate cut every year for a decade, from $1.145 to $0.805, worth about $2,650 a year on the county’s average home; and the Revenue Stabilization Fund, created in 2023 and holding about $120 million against a shortfall in the industry’s revenue.
items.summary: Voters in ten states limited data centers while the offers carried revenue the towns do not collect. The ballot record and the tax record, side by side.

items.title: The Distributed Machine: Redundancy Becomes the Architecture
items.content_html:
Breaking Report

The Infrastructure File — The Architecture of the Data Center

Objective

The Distributed Machine: Redundancy Becomes the Architecture

Telephony and computing began in single rooms, served through hierarchies. A century of automation, copying, and routing moved the service into the network itself. The record runs from the La Porte exchange of 1892 to the availability zones of 2026, and it lands on a buildout now contested site by site.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1105 ET, Friday, November 6, 2026.

The News in the File

The newest data-center plan in the record is not a campus. It is a scatter. Trade accounts filed on Friday, November 6, reported that Nvidia is examining a plan with the fiber carrier Brightspeed to place small data centers in more than 130 former telephone buildings across the United States—sites that already hold power connections and fiber—for a combined capacity reported at up to one gigawatt. Inside the project, according to the same accounts, the arrangement is described as an inference network: computing placed in many small facilities near the people requesting it, rather than in a few large ones far away. The companies have issued no announcement; the desk files the item as reported, and grades it again in the cocked hat below. The plan is filed here because of its shape. The shape is the subject of this report: the industry’s unit of construction is changing from the building to the network.

The counts describe the same change at the largest scale. Synergy Research Group counted 1,297 operational hyperscale data centers worldwide in late 2025, nearly triple the number of early 2018, with 770 more in planning, construction, or fit-out. Amazon Web Services operates 38 regions; Microsoft closed 2025 with more than 70 Azure regions and more than 400 data centers; Google Cloud stood at 42 regions and 127 zones. The facilities differ in size and owner. The architecture they share is the point: capacity held in many places at once, data copied between them as a matter of routine, and no single address at which the service lives.

The Single Room: Computing as It Began

Commercial computing began as one machine in one room, and the room was the service. IBM announced the System/360 family in April 1964, a line of compatible mainframes on which a customer’s programs could run across models. The machines stood in air-conditioned rooms, attended by operators, and the work arrived as decks of cards and left as printed paper. Time-sharing, added to the line with the Model 67 in 1966, let many users work at the same machine in the same hour. The user’s furniture was a terminal: in the 1970s, characteristically, an IBM 3270 display—a screen and keyboard with no computing of its own, which collected a full screen of entries and sent it to the mainframe when the operator pressed Enter. The arrangement was efficient and entirely dependent. A mainframe of the period could serve thousands of terminal users, and every one of them was served from the single room, or not at all.

Telephony began the same way, in a single room of a different kind. In the manual exchange, every call passed through an operator seated at a cord board, who took the request by voice and completed the connection by hand, plugging one cord into the jack of the calling line and another into the jack of the called line. The network above the local board was arranged as a hierarchy of five classes of office, from the Class 5 end office that served subscribers up through toll and primary and sectional centers to the Class 1 regional centers; tandem offices connected end offices to one another and to the levels above. The system’s research arm, Bell Telephone Laboratories, began moving to Murray Hill, New Jersey, in 1941; the transistor was demonstrated at Murray Hill in 1947. The hierarchy was orderly and it was a chain: each level depended on the level above it, and the operator’s hands were the switching fabric of the whole.

The Operator Leaves the Path

The first break in the chain was mechanical. Almon Strowger’s step-by-step switch, patented in 1891, let the caller’s own dial pulses move the switch directly, digit by digit, with no operator in the path. The first commercial step-by-step exchange opened at La Porte, Indiana, on November 3, 1892. The Bell System’s crossbar switch followed: the No. 1 Crossbar was installed at the Troy Avenue office in Brooklyn in 1938, and the No. 5 Crossbar, first installed at Media, Pennsylvania, in 1948, became the workhorse of the system. In 1965 the No. 1 Electronic Switching System put a stored program—a computer—in charge of the connections. Each step removed a pair of hands and a single point of attention from the path of a call. Switching became a function the network performed on itself, in every office at once, and the five-class hierarchy flattened as the offices grew able to reach one another directly.

The lesson the telephone network taught was structural, and computing learned it twice. A service concentrated in one room fails with the room. A service performed by a hierarchy fails at the level that fails. The systems that replaced both arrangements distributed the work itself—first the switching, then the content, then the computing—until the service no longer had a single address at which it could be interrupted.

The CDN Turn: Copies Near the Reader

The distribution of content began as an answer to a crowd. In 1995 Tim Berners-Lee challenged colleagues at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology to solve the congestion of a popular web site—the flash crowd that arrived at one server at one address and overwhelmed it. Tom Leighton, an MIT professor of applied mathematics, and Daniel Lewin, his graduate student, answered with consistent hashing, a method of spreading content across many servers so that the set could grow, shrink, and lose members without re-mapping the whole. Akamai Technologies was incorporated on August 20, 1998, by Leighton and Lewin with Jonathan Seelig and Randall Kaplan. The name is the Hawaiian word akamai: intelligent, clever—colloquially, cool.

The content delivery network changed where a web page lives. Under the Akamai model, copies of a publisher’s content are held on servers placed inside many networks, near the readers. A request is answered by a nearby copy. The publisher’s origin server remains, but it is no longer the place the public visits; it is the place the copies are made from. The failure arithmetic changed with the geography: a server under a flash crowd is one copy among many, and a server that fails removes one copy, not the publication. Within its first years Akamai was, by the accounts of the period, effectively the content delivery industry; the architecture it sold—many copies, served locally, refreshed from an origin—became the default shape of the public web.

The Modern Form: Zones, Regions, and One Address Everywhere

The hyperscalers applied the same principle to computing itself, and wrote it into their operating instructions. Amazon Web Services divides its infrastructure into Regions, each physically and logically independent, and each Region into three or more Availability Zones. An Availability Zone is one or more discrete data centers, physically separated from the zones beside it, with independent power, cooling, and network connections. AWS’s published reliability guidance instructs customers to deploy production workloads across at least two zones and to replicate data between them; the zones sit close enough for synchronous replication at single-digit-millisecond latency, so a copy is current, not eventual. Several of the company’s largest storage and database services replicate across zones by default. The design objective, in the document’s own terms, is the avoidance of single points of failure, including the underlying physical infrastructure.

Cloudflare carries the principle into the network’s addressing. Its network runs on anycast: every location announces the same IP addresses, and the internet’s routing delivers each request to the nearest location able to answer it. Cloudflare’s own documentation states the failure behavior plainly: because multiple nodes advertise the same address, if one node fails, requests are routed to another node in close proximity. There is no failover address to publish and no single facility whose loss changes the address of the service. The company reports data centers in 335 cities. The service is the address; the address is everywhere the network is.

The storage industry had named the underlying principle a generation earlier, and the facility now follows the disk. RAID arrays, standardized in the late 1980s, write data across multiple disks so that the failure of one disk is an event, not a loss; backup practice added copies held in different places against the failure of the building itself. The desk prints the analogy as an analogy, because it is exact at the level of design: the unit of engineering is no longer the single store of the data but the set of copies, the rules that keep them in agreement, and the routing that finds a surviving copy when one is gone. A modern data center is built the way the array was: replaceable, replicated, and one member of a set.

The Contested Ground, and the Structural Answer

The construction program is contested at the level of the individual site, and the record of the contest is counted. On November 3, voters in ten states decided 41 local measures on data-center construction; in Ballotpedia’s complete tracker, 40 went the way of tighter limits. Data Center Watch, as reported by Data Center Knowledge, counted more than 36 projects representing $162 billion of investment blocked or significantly delayed as of June 2025. Site selection has adjusted its vocabulary to the record: an industry account of 2026 practice describes the discipline as deliverability—the overlap of entitled land, available power, and a local community willing to partner on the project—and describes the market splitting into two tracks, hyperscale campuses of hundreds of megawatts and hyperlocal sites of one to twenty megawatts close to users.

Distribution is the architecture’s answer to a refusal, and the answer is mechanical rather than rhetorical. A workload deployed across zones and regions under the operators’ own published guidance does not have a hometown. Capacity refused in one jurisdiction is capacity placed in another; a site that is delayed delays one member of a set whose other members continue. The reported Nvidia–Brightspeed plan is the limiting case of the same logic: capacity distributed across more than 130 existing buildings, each individually small, each already holding the power and fiber connections a new campus waits years to obtain, and none of them individually the network. The data center began as a palace built to hold a unique machine. The record of 2026 shows it completing the telephone network’s migration: from the single room, to the hierarchy, to the network of copies—a service that persists because no one place is the service.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. The scale figures carry one. The desk’s sources put Amazon’s footprint at 38 regions with 120 availability zones in one October 2026 accounting and at 38 regions with more than 100 zones in another; the counts were taken at different dates against a buildout adding zones continuously, and they agree on the structure while differing on the count. The Friday item carries a wider triangle: the Nvidia–Brightspeed plan rests on trade reporting that the companies have not confirmed in any announcement the desk can file, and its figures—130 buildings, one gigawatt—are the reported figures of a plan under examination, not of a construction program under way. The historical bearings are single-valued: the La Porte exchange opened on November 3, 1892; Akamai was incorporated on August 20, 1998; the No. 1 Crossbar went in at Brooklyn in 1938. The architecture those dates produced is the single-valued fact underneath the triangle of counts: the copies are the system now. The log proceeds to the Midday Watch.

The Clippings Filed With This Report

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only part of this file stamped objective. Eight items.

Subjective
Amazon Web Services — deploy the workload to multiple locations

The operator’s own reliability guidance: each Region physically and logically independent and made of three or more Availability Zones; zones physically separated and isolated, with independent power and network; data replicated synchronously between zones; production workloads to run in at least two zones; the stated design principle is the avoidance of single points of failure, the physical infrastructure included.

Subjective
Cloudflare — what anycast is, in the operator’s account

The operator’s explainer of its own architecture: one IP address applied to many servers, queries answered by the closest, availability preserved when a resolver goes offline because others answer, and the network stated at 335 cities. The desk’s report takes the mechanism and the failure behavior from this account and prints the city count as the operator’s own figure.

Subjective
Data Center Knowledge — the hyperscalers in 2026

The trade paper’s state of the buildout: 1,297 operational hyperscale data centers counted by Synergy Research Group in late 2025 and 770 in the pipeline; Amazon at 38 regions, Microsoft past 70 regions and 400 data centers, Google at 42 regions and 127 zones; and Data Center Watch’s count of more than 36 projects, $162 billion of investment, blocked or significantly delayed as of June 2025.

Subjective
Softonic — the reported Nvidia and Brightspeed plan

Friday’s account of the reported plan: more than 130 former telecom buildings to be used as small data centers, reusing sites that already have power and fiber, the portfolio reaching about one gigawatt, and the arrangement described inside the project as an inference network for live requests close to users. The item is reported rather than announced, and the report above files it as such.

Subjective
Knowledge at Wharton — Akamai’s founding

The business school’s account of the company’s start: the name Hawaiian for intelligent and clever; the product a mathematical algorithm, developed at MIT under Tom Leighton, routing content to servers that forward it to the end user; the company founded by Leighton with Daniel Lewin, his graduate student, after Tim Berners-Lee’s challenge on internet congestion.

Subjective
Telephone World — the switch timeline

The dated record of the switching succession: the Strowger switch patented in 1891 and its first commercial exchange at La Porte, Indiana, on November 3, 1892; the first No. 1 Crossbar at Brooklyn in 1938; crossbar tandem in 1941; the No. 5 Crossbar at Media, Pennsylvania, in 1948. The report’s automation dates are taken from this file.

Subjective
Route Fifty — voters reject data centers in local initiatives

The election account of the local votes: more than forty measures across ten states, the opponents of data-center development successful in virtually all of them, Ohio carrying the most initiatives, some votes advisory rather than binding, and a single locality where the facilities prevailed. Ballotpedia’s complete count, forty-one measures and forty for tighter limits, is the figure the report prints.

Subjective
Inflect — site selection in 2026

An industry account of how sites are now chosen: the field splitting into hyperscale campuses of hundreds of megawatts and hyperlocal sites of one to twenty megawatts; deliverability defined as the overlap of entitled land, available power, and a community willing to partner; and demand pushing activity into secondary markets as primary markets fill.
items.summary: Mainframes and cord boards gave way to Akamai, anycast, and availability zones. The record of how computing left the single room and learned to keep copies.

items.title: Tokyo Closes in a Bear Market, Brent Crosses a Hundred, and the Count Waits
items.content_html:
The Night File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

Tokyo Closes in a Bear Market, Brent Crosses a Hundred, and the Count Waits

At 0400 the night’s work is finished in Asia and not begun in Washington. Tokyo and Seoul have closed about 6 percent lower, Brent has briefly crossed $100 a barrel on the tanker file and stands just under it, gold has fallen with the shares it usually shelters from, the president has said he will soon decide whether to resume all-out war in Iran, and no race was called in the night. Friday’s first American fact is set for 0830: the October payrolls report.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0400 ET, Friday, November 6, 2026. This edition continues the log from Edition No. 9, the Midnight Watch, which carried Asia’s Friday session in its morning state. The closes printed here replace the morning figures; the midnight edition stands unrevised, as a log stands.

The Night in Brief

No race was called in the night, in either chamber, in any state. The Senate stands where it has stood since Wednesday: 54 seats for the Democrats and 44 for the Republicans, with Alaska and Mississippi uncalled. The governorships stand at 28 for the Democrats, with Alaska and Kansas open. Colorado’s 4th District stands in its latest state with the Democrat ahead by 3,024 votes and the race uncalled. What moved in the night was not the count. It was the price of the election, taken a second time in Asia and closed there; the price of oil, carried back over $100 and held just under it; and the war, on which the president, meeting his national security team for the first time since the vote, said a decision is coming soon. The desk files those three in that order.

Asia Closes: Tokyo in a Bear Market, Seoul Off the Floor

Asia’s Friday session is closed, and the closes are the night’s largest settled fact. In Tokyo the Nikkei 225 closed down 3,666.99 points, or 6.00 percent—at 57,410.91 in the closing account carrying the market data filed below, at 57,434.70 in the Tokyo–Seoul closing account, and at 57,420.23 in the morning brief. The three figures differ in the last digits; the fall, the worst day since April 2025 per Dow Jones Newswires’ closing update, does not. The index had closed above 72,000 for the first time in late June; a close more than 20 percent below that record puts it in a bear market, and every closing account records it there. SoftBank Group fell more than 10 percent in the Dow Jones figures and 10.83 percent to 3,549 yen in the closing account; Kioxia fell 8.72 percent to 8,511 yen.

Seoul closed off its floor, after a halt and an emergency meeting. The Kospi fell more than 8 percent in the morning, to an intraday low of 4,911.28, broke below 5,000 for the first time since February 6, and triggered a Level 1 circuit breaker at 9:03 a.m. that halted trading for 20 minutes—the eleventh breaker of the year, per the Seoul closing account filed below. The government convened an emergency meeting to review market conditions, support buying followed, and the index closed down 324.11 points, or 6.02 percent, at 5,059.69; the closing account’s last figure is 5,059.65. Samsung Electronics closed down 6.35 percent at 188,700 won, and SK Hynix down 10.44 percent to 1,132,000 won. The Kosdaq closed down 5.03 percent at 644.27. Of the twenty largest stocks in Seoul, only Naver rose, up 2.87 percent. In Taipei the Taiex ended 4.5 percent lower, its largest daily fall since July, with TSMC down 4.7 percent; the Hang Seng Tech Index was 1.8 percent lower; Singapore’s Straits Times Index was 2.9 percent lower in the Dow Jones update’s last state. The reason the accounts give is the reason Thursday gave in New York: the Democratic victory, read as regulation and delay for the data-center buildout Asia supplies, priced into the same chip names on the next day’s date. No new American fact arrived in the night to change that reading, and none was needed.

The Futures, and the Test at 0830

The American futures spent the night in two directions, and the desk prints both states with their hours. In the early evening, carrying CNBC’s figures, the futures account filed below recorded S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 futures each down 0.4 percent and Dow futures down 201 points. In the early European hours, the later futures account recorded Dow futures down 0.85 percent at about 51,170, S&P 500 futures up 0.06 percent at about 7,390, and Nasdaq 100 futures up 0.90 percent at about 26,990. A bounce in the Nasdaq contracts and a fall in the Dow contracts is not a recovery and not a rout; it is a market waiting, and what it is waiting for is printed on the calendar. The October employment report is due at 0830 ET. The Dow Jones consensus stands at 59,000 jobs added, against 29,000 in September, with the unemployment rate expected to hold at 4.2 percent; the forecasts on the shelf run from about 55,000 to 65,000, and the private ADP report, already in, stands at 86,000 against 75,000 expected. The report is the first hard labor figure since the sell-off, and it lands in front of the Federal Reserve’s December 9 meeting, at which traders price the chance of a further 25-basis-point increase between 67 and about 70 percent in the files on the shelf.

Oil: Brent Crosses a Hundred, and Holds Just Under It

Brent crossed $100 in the morning trade in Asia and did not hold the round number. Reuters’ Beijing and Perth file records January Brent up $1.29, or 1.31 percent, at $99.58 a barrel as of 0504 GMT, briefly breaching $100 in morning trade, and West Texas Intermediate up 86 cents, or 0.95 percent, at $91.38. A later account, carrying CNBC’s figures at 0730 GMT, puts Brent at $99.90, up 1.67 percent, and West Texas Intermediate at $91.69. Thursday’s settlement stands beneath both: Brent at $98.29, up $3.67, and West Texas Intermediate at $90.52. The week’s bearing stands in the same files and does not move: both benchmarks remain on course for a fall of about 12 percent on the week, after Wednesday’s 8 percent fall on the election result. The rebound is two days old and is carried, in every account, by the same cargo: the tanker attacks in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, and the finding, stated by ANZ’s senior commodity strategist in the files, that flows through the strait are running at under 60 percent of capacity. Against the rebound, JPMorgan’s estimate, carried in the oil account filed below, is that supply exceeded demand by 1.1 million barrels a day in September and by 1.4 million in October. Both facts are in the price at 0400: a strait at three-fifths flow, and a world producing more oil than it burns.

The Strait, and the Decision the President Says Is Coming

The tanker file did not grow in the night; the decision file did. The claims stand where the midnight edition left them: Iran reported three more tankers attacked in the strait on Thursday, on top of the Guards’ report of two tankers and a tugboat catching fire, and the British agency UKMTO’s count stands at at least five vessels reporting incidents since Sunday, at close to the record pace of October. No independent confirmation of the Thursday incidents appears in any file the desk took in the night. What the night added is the president, on the record, in the Oval Office on Thursday, after meeting his national security team on Iran for the first time since the elections. The account of the meeting, carrying Axios’s reporting filed below, records his words: “Now we will make a decision.” Asked whether to go further with strikes to ensure Iran’s nuclear program is dead and that “it will never happen again,” he said: “I would rather not destroy the rest of the country if possible, but maybe I will have to. You’ll know soon enough.” The options before him are stated in the same account as three: new strikes, continued economic pressure, or a deal carrying significant concessions. Central Command is finalizing preparations to resume major combat operations and has received no new directive, per an American official in the account; a third carrier group, led by the USS Theodore Roosevelt, is due in Singapore on Friday for a port call and cannot reach the region before mid-November.

The mediation now has a printed shape, and Tehran’s answer to it was delivered in Moscow. The Qatari mediators’ draft, in the same account, runs on two days: on the first, the United States lifts its naval blockade and releases some of Iran’s frozen funds, and Iran invites the International Atomic Energy Agency to send inspectors to the bombed nuclear sites; on the second, the Strait of Hormuz reopens, and nuclear talks resume on Iran’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium. Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, spent Thursday in calls with mediators from Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, Oman, and Egypt. Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, spent it at the Kremlin, delivering a message from the supreme leader to President Putin, who stated his readiness to help end the war. Rezaei’s statement after the meeting is the night’s second fixed point: “We told Mr. Putin that we announced seven conditions to the Americans regarding diplomacy, and that until the Americans fulfill our seven conditions, neither the Strait of Hormuz will be opened nor will there be any negotiations.” A separate file records that Iran returned a copy of one nuclear proposal to the United States through the Qatari mediators on Thursday. No agreement was announced. The two tracks—a two-day draft in Doha and seven conditions in Moscow—are both on paper at 0400, and they do not describe the same distance.

The Count at 0400, and the Business of Friday

The count did not move in the night, and its latest states are printed for the record. The Associated Press Senate file in its latest state lists Alaska too early to call at 73.95 percent of precincts reporting and Mississippi too early to call at 99.83 percent. The margins underneath them stand as the earlier editions printed them: in Mississippi the Democrat, Scott Colom, ahead of the incumbent Republican, Cindy Hyde-Smith, by 1,138 votes in the Associated Press figures of November 5 and by 1,824 in Decision Desk HQ’s later figures, with other files running the lead from a few dozen votes to just over a thousand—a spread the desk prints rather than resolves; in Alaska the Democrat, Mary Peltola, ahead of the incumbent Republican, Dan Sullivan, by 626 to 637 first-choice votes, with a second candidate named Daniel Sullivan holding more votes than the margin. The dates govern: Mississippi’s affidavit identification is due November 10 and its counties certify by November 13, and the candidate with the most votes wins; Alaska’s ranked-choice tabulation is set for November 18. In Colorado’s 4th District the wire’s latest state, carried in the state results file updated at 6:25 p.m. MST, puts the Democrat, Eileen Laubacher, at 184,103 votes and the incumbent Republican, Lauren Boebert, at 181,079—a margin of 3,024, with 96.89 percent of precincts reporting and the race uncalled. Weld County, the incumbent’s strongest, has finished its ordinary counting; what remains sits largely in counties the challenger is carrying, and the cure and overseas deadline is November 12.

Friday’s Washington business is a deadline, not a session. Candidates for the House Republican leadership elections must declare by noon today. The field as filed stands: Speaker Mike Johnson will not seek the minority leadership; Majority Leader Steve Scalise and Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan are declared for it; Majority Whip Tom Emmer seeks to remain whip and is challenged by August Pfluger; and the elections are set for Tuesday, November 10. On the other side of the chamber, Hakeem Jeffries has sought his colleagues’ support to become Speaker when the new Congress convenes on January 3. Congress itself returns Monday, November 9, to the lame-duck session, funded through December 11. None of that business was transacted in the night. It is filed here because Friday will transact the first of it before the Midday Watch collects.

Gold Falls With the Shares; Europe Waits to Open

Gold did the unusual thing in the night: it fell while the shares fell. Spot gold slipped 0.6 percent to $4,063.39 an ounce by 0248 GMT and December futures fell 1 percent to $4,072.90, per the gold account filed below; the Dow Jones closing update records precious metals swept up as investors sold positions to cover losses elsewhere. The metal had touched $4,146.63 on Thursday, a high of more than two weeks, and stands about 4 percent higher on the week even after the fall. Goldman Sachs on Thursday cut its end-of-2026 target by $500, to $4,150 an ounce from $4,650. Silver rose 0.3 percent to $51.91. The accounts give the same two reasons for gold’s fall as for oil’s rise: crude back toward $100 carries an inflation reading with it, and an inflation reading carries the expectation of higher American rates, which is the weather gold does not like. Europe, at 0400, has not opened. Its futures have: contracts on the EURO STOXX 50 were down 1 percent at 0652 GMT, with German contracts down 0.8 percent and British down 0.9 percent, per the Reuters account of the European open filed below. The STOXX 600 stands, in that account, up more than 1.3 percent on the week and just over 1 percent from a record high, carrying less of the AI trade than the indexes that fell in New York and Tokyo. Whether that shelter holds is the European session’s question, and it belongs to the Midday Watch.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. First, Tokyo’s close: 57,410.91, 57,420.23, and 57,434.70 in three closing files, a spread of 24 points on a fall of 3,667—the level agreed, the last digits not. Second, the futures: down across the board in the early-evening account, split in the early-European account, Dow down and Nasdaq up—two states of one unsettled night, printed with their hours because the hour is the difference. Third, Mississippi: a Democratic lead of a few dozen votes in one file, 1,138 in the wire’s, 1,824 in the decision desk’s, each taken at a different stage of the same unfinished count. Fourth, Brent: $99.58 at 0504 GMT, $99.86 in an earlier overnight state, $99.90 at 0730 GMT, and $100 crossed briefly between them—one rising market read at four hours. Against the triangle, the load-bearing facts of the night are single-valued: Asia is closed and down about 6 percent in Tokyo and Seoul; the Nikkei is in a bear market; Brent settled Thursday at $98.29 and trades just under $100; gold stands at about $4,063; no race was called; the president said a decision on Iran is coming soon and named no date; Tehran’s seven conditions stand unwithdrawn; and the payrolls report is due at 0830. The log proceeds to Friday.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. Twenty-nine items.

Subjective
Dow Jones Newswires, via Morningstar — Asian equities tumble as the AI selloff deepens

Friday’s closes in the update timed 02:15 ET: the Kospi down as much as 8.8 percent in the session and finished 6.0 percent lower, with weekly losses of 12 percent; the Nikkei below 60,000 and closed 6.0 percent lower in its worst day since April 2025; the Taiex 4.5 percent lower; SK Hynix down over 10 percent, SoftBank down over 10 percent, TSMC down 4.7 percent; the Hang Seng Tech Index 1.8 percent lower; gold down 1 percent as positions were sold to cover losses; Brent up 1.7 percent and reclaiming $100 in its figures; and the ANZ analysts’ sentence that the reality of the situation hit home, with Iran still holding the Strait of Hormuz.

Subjective
Reuters, via EuropeSays — Asia stocks crumble after the AI rout

Filed from Singapore on November 6: Asia’s tech-heavy markets sank as fear of regulatory scrutiny and a slowdown in the AI build-out followed the steepest fall in American stocks since the tariff rout of a year and a half before; the Kospi down more than 8 percent with a 20-minute circuit-breaker halt and the Nikkei down 5 percent at the file’s hour; $3 trillion wiped off S&P 500 companies; the semiconductor index down 12.2 percent overnight and the Nasdaq 12 percent below its record close of a month before; and the Singapore and Sydney analysts’ readings of a shift in sentiment.

Subjective
TradingKey — the Kospi reclaims 5,000, Tokyo and Seoul pare their losses

The closing account: the Kospi down more than 8 percent intraday, below 5,000, with a 20-minute circuit breaker, then support buying from the National Pension Service and other institutions, closing down 6.02 percent at 5,059.65; Samsung Electronics down 6.35 percent at 188,700 won and SK Hynix down 10.44 percent at 1,132,000 won; the Nikkei gapped below 60,000 and closed down 5.96 percent at 57,434.70, with Kioxia down 8.72 percent at 8,511 yen and SoftBank down 10.83 percent at 3,549 yen.

Subjective
Seoul Economic Daily — the Kospi plunges 6.02 percent to close at 5,059.69

The close recorded in one line: the Kospi at 5,059.69, down 324.11 points, or 6.02 percent.

Subjective
Money Today — the Kospi closes above 5,000 after the breaker

The Seoul close in full: the Kospi at 5,059.69, down 6.02 percent, after a low of 4,911.28, the first intraday break of 5,000 since February 6; a Stage 1 circuit breaker at 9:03 a.m. halting trading for 20 minutes; the Kosdaq at 644.27, down 5.03 percent; Naver the only riser among the twenty largest stocks, up 2.87 percent; and the won closing its day session at 1,342.1 to the dollar in the same account.

Subjective
KuCoin News, carrying Huo Xing Finance — the Nikkei falls 6 percent into a bear market

The closing figures in one file: the Nikkei 225 down 3,666.99 points, or 6.00 percent, at 57,410.91, more than 20 percent below its June closing peak and in a technical bear market; the Kospi down 324.15 points, or 6.02 percent, at 5,059.65, after a morning fall of more than 8 percent, a break of 5,000, and its eleventh circuit breaker of the year; the South Korean government’s emergency market meeting, after which the decline narrowed; the Kosdaq down 5 percent; SK Hynix down over 10 percent and Samsung Electronics down 6.35 percent.

Subjective
Samuel & Co Trading — Asia catches the Nasdaq correction, the morning brief for November 6

The brief’s view: the Nikkei closed at 57,420.23, down 5.99 percent and into bear-market territory; the Kospi fell 5.41 percent to 5,092.38 in its figures after a worse open; American futures trying a mild bounce into Friday, with S&P futures near 7,388.50, Nasdaq 100 futures near 27,009, and Dow futures near 51,139 in the London morning; about $3 trillion wiped off S&P 500 firms on Thursday; and the payrolls report named as the dial that settles whether Thursday was a one-day fall or the start of a deeper unwind, with December hike odds at roughly 70 percent.

Subjective
The Hindu BusinessLine — the Nikkei plunges, the Kospi falls, in the morning state

The Asian session at midday, updated November 6 at 08:52: the Nikkei 5.7 percent lower at 57,576.63 by midday after a fall of more than 6 percent at the open; the Kospi down 7.4 percent to 4,985.99, with Samsung Electronics down 7.9 percent in the morning; Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 down 1.0 percent to 8,973.00; the Hang Seng down 0.7 percent to 24,630.03 and the Shanghai Composite down 1.3 percent to 3,642.10; and Nvidia named as the heaviest weight on the S&P 500 on Thursday.

Subjective
The Business Standard — the Democrats’ win spooks AI investors

The rout and its cause in one file: investors worried the party will use its gains in Congress and the state capitols to regulate and slow the AI build-out; the Nasdaq down 5.56 percent in its figures, its most dramatic fall in 19 months, two days after Democrats flipped seven Senate seats, gained at least 39 in the House, and picked up five governorships; and the Alaska and Mississippi races still uncalled, with the majority’s possible rise to 56–44 stated.

Subjective
Reuters, via 98.5 The River — oil set for a sharp weekly drop, supply concerns a floor

Beijing and Perth, November 6: January Brent up $1.29, or 1.31 percent, to $99.58 a barrel as of 0504 GMT, briefly breaching $100 in morning trade, and West Texas Intermediate up 86 cents, or 0.95 percent, to $91.38, both up for a second day; Brent on track to fall 12 percent on the week and West Texas Intermediate 12.1 percent; Wednesday’s 8 percent fall on the election result, and the rebound on the surge of tanker attacks on Wednesday and Thursday; Iran’s report of three more tankers attacked and UKMTO’s near-record pace; and the KCM analyst’s reading of a technical recovery over a problem that has not disappeared.

Subjective
FinanceFeeds — Brent at $99.90 on Friday morning

Updated November 6 at 07:30 GMT, carrying CNBC’s figures: Brent up 1.67 percent to $99.90 a barrel and West Texas Intermediate up 1.43 percent to $91.69; Brent still heading for a weekly loss of about 12 percent; the reference levels stated at $93.50 below and $103.60 above; Iran’s three more reported tanker attacks on Thursday and UKMTO’s near-record rate; flows through the strait at less than 60 percent of capacity in the ANZ strategist’s figure; and the October jobs report named as the day’s demand question.

Subjective
Invezz — Brent nears $100 despite a 12 percent weekly slump

November 6, 01:43: Brent up 1.31 percent to $99.58 at 0504 GMT after briefly crossing $100, and West Texas Intermediate up 0.95 percent to $91.38, with both benchmarks still on course for weekly losses of around 12 percent; tanker attacks near the strait keeping a risk premium in the price while hopes of an easing of the war pull the other way; flows through the strait below 60 percent of capacity in the ANZ estimate; and JPMorgan’s estimate that supply exceeded demand by 1.1 million barrels a day in September, widening to 1.4 million in October.

Subjective
The Hindu BusinessLine — crude gains amid fresh tanker attacks

Friday morning in the Indian market’s figures: January Brent at $99.83, up 1.57 percent, at 10:04 a.m., and December West Texas Intermediate at $91.73, up 1.34 percent, after Brent crossed $99; UKMTO’s reports of tanker attacks in the Gulf and the strait since Sunday; and the Revolutionary Guards’ report of two oil tankers and a tugboat catching fire in separate incidents in the strait.

Subjective
OilPrice — oil heads for a 12 percent weekly loss despite fresh tanker attacks

Brent at $99.42 and West Texas Intermediate at $91.242 at the file’s hour, both up from Thursday’s close on reports of fresh tanker attacks; both benchmarks down 12 percent since Monday on hopes the midterm result brings a swift end to the war; at least five vessel incidents in the Gulf since Sunday in the Reuters figures carried in the story; and shipments through the strait recovering while threats to commercial traffic persist.

Subjective
Axios, via Zot — the president says he will soon decide on resuming all-out war

The Thursday meeting and the diplomacy in one file: the president’s first meeting with his national security team on Iran since the elections, held as part of his weekly intelligence briefing; his words in the Oval Office—“Now we will make a decision,” and “I would rather not destroy the rest of the country if possible, but maybe I will have to. You’ll know soon enough”; the three options of new strikes, economic pressure, or a deal with significant concessions; Central Command finalizing preparations without a new directive, and the USS Theodore Roosevelt due in Singapore on Friday, unable to reach the region before mid-November; the Qatari two-day draft—blockade lifted and frozen funds released and inspectors invited on the first day, the strait reopened and nuclear talks resumed on the second; Araghchi’s calls with six regional mediators; and Rezaei at the Kremlin, delivering the supreme leader’s message, stating the seven conditions to President Putin, and Putin’s readiness to help end the war.

Subjective
New York Post — the commander’s podcast, as the president weighs his next move

Iran reviewing American-backed proposals on its nuclear program, with at least three meetings on concrete proposals in the past week in Tehran and Doha through Qatari mediators, and Iran returning a copy of one nuclear proposal to the United States through the mediators on Thursday, per the Reuters reporting carried in the story; the president’s Oval Office sentence on destroying the rest of the country; the June memorandum that collapsed over shipping routes in the strait; the parliament speaker’s charge that the president is preparing the next phase of the war; and, in the same file, Central Command’s commander launching a podcast on Thursday with jokes about French fries and retiring to play basketball.

Subjective
Reuters, via The Business Standard — tankers hit in Hormuz as Iran keeps up pressure

Dubai, November 5: Iran reported three more tankers damaged in the strait on Thursday; at least five vessels reporting incidents since Sunday in UKMTO’s count, against 35 vessels hit in October, the most of any month of the war; Qatar’s statement that the United States and Iran are reviewing proposals to bridge their differences, with no breakthrough announced; the vice president’s blame of the war for the defeat and the president’s defense of it; the two unnamed sources’ statement that the president is planning to bomb Iran and held off for the midterms; and the four subjects of the peacemaking—the strait, the blockade, sanctions, and the nuclear program.

Subjective
Associated Press — Senate, every state

The Senate file in its latest state: 35 races listed, Alaska too early to call at 73.95 percent of precincts reporting and Mississippi too early to call at 99.83 percent, and the remaining races called state by state.

Subjective
ASEAN Now, carrying the agencies — Alaska and Mississippi to decide the strength of the majority

Days after the vote, the two Senate races remain uncalled and will determine the size of the Democratic majority: in Mississippi, Colom leading Hyde-Smith by just over 1,000 votes with counting continuing, in a state the president carried by 20 points in 2024, and the lead narrowing in Decision Desk HQ’s figures at more than 95 percent counted; in Alaska, Peltola at 48.2 percent to Sullivan’s 47.9 with about 69 percent counted in the file’s figures, with the governorship and the ballot measure on the state’s primary and ranked-choice system also uncalled.

Subjective
